summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 representing interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax officer included a further sum of RS. 1.50,500 representing interest accrued on the amount of the assessee on accrual basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessment of the assesee. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the assessee was assessable to wealth Tax for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the deceased if he were alive. The system of accounting mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the assesses. That appears plainly from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value of all the assets" belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date. All the assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the value date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in that property. [310B C] 1.2 The system accounting mercantile, mercantile or hydrid is no relevance to the purpose for determining the asset of theassessee. That seems plainly from section 7 as the valuation dates the last day of the income tax "previous year" stops there. The method of accounting, mercantile and cash or Hybrid, is of any relevance for determining assets of an assessee.

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ing employees of the project. The respondent was charge sheeted by the Personnel Officer of the Project for having committed misconduct by impersonation. The Inquiry Officer framed charges against him. The Enquiry Officer held that he had committed misconduct in preparing the Pay Roll pertaining to 'Token of Central Survey Division, Sunder Nagar during the month of May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty as mate in devotion to duties as mates in his service book. He made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month May 1969 failing which he was liable to be dismissed from service. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the legality of the order of dismissal and also the punishment awarded to him. A Single Judge of the High Cour t, who heard the matter, held that the respondent was guilty of entering the name of Ashoka Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 or that it was he who had initiated identity card. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal filed by the appel lant holding that the respond ent was guilty and there were others too, and as such, he should not be granted a lesser punishment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court or the Tribunal has no juris diction to interfere with the penalty if the findings recorded as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed are placed, it is not for the Court to consider whether the ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in dismissing the public servant. [534B C] 1.2. The Tribunal cannot substitute its own judgment to modi fied penalty where there are some relevant materials whi ch the authority has accepted and materials which may be relied upon by a Tribunal for its conclusion. If the High court is satisfied that some but not all of them is irrelevant or irrelevant, it would be impossible for a superior Court to find out of which reasons, relevant or irrelevant or invalid, valid or irrelevant if another ground by itself was serious en quence before the Tribunal even if some of it was found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. This Court in Shankar Dass vs Union of India, ; , held that where there were some relevant material whi th e authority had accepted and material which may have weighed with the authorit y, the penalty could not be imposed on the proved misconduct. [511E F] 1:3. The adequacy of penalty unless it is certain malafide is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of the ap pellate authority. If there has been an enquiry consist ing of evidence even if any of it is found to he irrelevant or relevant, valid, invalid or irrelevant t hey, relevant and there is nothing to show that the authori ty would have passed the order on the basis of the other relevant and existing grounds. On the other hand, an order basi sion which is not a matter for the Tribunal to concern with. The sufficiency of penalty must depend upon the circumstances of each case.

The appellant filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The respondents resisted the suit on the ground that the appellant was not in lawful possession of the said property and since he had not been dispossessed, in accordance with law, his tenancy having been lawfully terminated, without his tenancy being lawfully terminated. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the decree passed by the Civil Court was unsustainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the civil court stood ousted by section 58(2) of Code of Criminal Procedure. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The suit was not barred by order 2 Rule 1(3). The question whether the appellant is a deemed tenancy or a tenant was not required to he decided by Civil Court under the Act and there was no express saving clause permitting the Civil court to decide the same. [1020E] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act. The question is whether the respondents were a tenant in respect of agricultural land would be within the exclusive jurisdiction of Mamlatdar under section 7 read with section 58 (2) and section 58 of the Civil Procedure Code. [1120F] 2:2.1 The jurisdiction of civil court is specifically barred by sub rule (2), which provides that a person entitled to more than one relief in respect thereof, if evicted from the land on or after 1st July 1962, such person shall be entitled to recover immediate possession of land in the manner prescribed by or under the Bombay Act unless the landlord proves that the termination of tenancy was in the way authorised by section 9. Even in cases of threatened wrongful dispossession section 8A says that any tenant in possession of any land or dwelling house who apprehends that he may be dispossessed contrary to the provisions of this Act may apply in writing for such possession to the Tehsildar. [1220G H] 2(a) The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 read and section 8(2), specifically bars the jurisdiction. If any question arises whether a landlord is a person or a protected tenant, the Civil Courts will continue to have jurisdiction. [1321B C] (b) In the present case, since the appellant has not applied for possession, there was a question of granting an injunction and the only relief which the court could have granted was in regard to the declaration sought which the Court could not hold against him as a mere declaration of his status as a tenant.

The petitioners are carpenters in the State of Himachal Pradesh. They claim for pay scale admissible to "Senior Speech Pathologist" and "Speech Pathologist". Their case was that they performed the same duties and performing similar functions as other drivers in the service of the Corporation. The Court found that the petitioners performed the duties and perform similar functions, as other driver in the Government service. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment is made bona fide, reasonably on an intelligible criterion which has a rational nexus with the object of dif ferentiation, such differentiation will not amount to discrimination. [668E F] 2. The principles of " Equal pay for unequal work" cannot be enforced invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. So as long as that value judgment was made bona fied bona fide reasonably on a intelligible criterion, which has rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved, efficiency in the administration, the State would be justified in prescribing different pay scales. [669F] 3. The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable to their counterparts in Government service, and they are being paid the minimum wages admissible to such workmen. The court, therefore, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of the Corpora tion. [670G] 4. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. Unless it is shown that there was a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the similar master in the same establishment, the principle of equal pay for Equal work cannot be invoked invariably in each kind of serv ice particularly in areas of professional service. [667A B] 5. The law relating to equal pay has practically been practically re hammered out and very little remains for further innovation. In the light of the aforesaid principles, it is not open to the State to classify employees on the basis of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned.

The prosecution alleged that on the fateful day between 1.1.1976 and 2.1, 1976 at Babultara village, the accused 1 to 4 committed murder of Parubai in pursuance of a conspiracy with the approver P.W. 1 for committing murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of Babultana village. The Sessions Judge found on a consideration of the evidence all the seven accused not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted them. He convicted the accused 6 and 7 under section 302 read with section 34 I. P.C., but acquitted them, holding that they were guilty of an offence under section 304A I.T.C.; and that they had been acquitted by the trial court. The High Court on appeal confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to the accused persons. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the conviction of one of the accused alone was unsustainable in law having regard to the requirement of section120A IP. C., and that the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 2, 4 and 7 could not be relied upon against them under section 34, I.I.P.,C. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not he relied upon by the prosecution on four pieces of evidence besides the evidence regarding recovery of the blood stained shirt, article 54 and the medical evidence of the approver. [784 D] (2) The High court was in error in holding that the guilt of accused 6 for the murder of Malan had been proved beyond all reasonable doubt.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will executed by her husband, executed a will in favour of her husband. The properties were bequeathed to her husband and she was given only a life interest in items 1 and 2. By his plaint the appellant claimed that the said Lakshmamma had transferred all her interest in the properties comprised in the said deed of gift in favour Of her husband 's husband, and that on her death the said items would vest in respondents 2 to 4 and respondent 5 respectively. The trial court held that the will was genuine and valid and that at the material time the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind and that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intentions. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that as the will set up by the husband was not proved to be the last will of the testator, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the document and to establish that Lakshmammal had really understood its contents, had approved of them and put her signatures on it when she was in sound disposing State of mind. Held, that the High court was right in reversing the finding of the trial court that the Will set up was the last Will of the executant. The testator 's evidence did not show satisfactorily that the testatrix had understood its content, and the effect of the dispositions made before her. It was not shown that the propounder had taken a prominent part in the execution and that she understood the nature and effect of its contents. That leaves the evidence of the scribe and the appellant himself. The High Court was therefore justified in reversing this finding of fact.

The Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, was amended by the Andhra Pradesh Act No. 26 of 1957, which came into force on September 9, 1963, and entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Act read as follows: "Cinematographic equipment including cameras, projectors, projector recording and sound reproducing equipment and sound recording and reproducing equipment". The appellant company was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No 4 of 1st schedule of the Andhra Act. The High Court held that the main use of the carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast through the projectors. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The entry in the schedule relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "component parts of motor vehicles". Entry No. 2 relating to "Motor vehicles", refers to "electrical apparatus" including "electricity accumulators, amplifiers and loud speakers". [562 B C] (2) The word "cinema carbonons" in the Schedule relates to `motor vehicle ' and includes `component part of motor vehicle '. Entry No 2 relating thereto refers to `electrical equipment and apparatus ' also. The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for dictaphones and other parts required for use therewith. Apparently, the factor deciding is the predominant or ordinary purpose or use. It is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses. [562 D E] (3) The expression "required for use" in Entry No 4 occurs at the end of the expression occurs at a later stage, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for use for a particular kind of instrument. It will be noticed that the entry refers to 'electrical appliances and other cameras and enlargers, films and plates, paper and cloth and other part parts required or accessories required for such use therewith". [563 B C; 564 A] (4) The words `parts ' in Entry 4 occurs in a schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for the use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster ' Third New International Dictionary as follows. "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that added to be theauty, convenience, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary something of greater or primary importance"; "additional" "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "Accessories" are not necessarily confined to particular machines for which they may serve as aids. The same item may be an accessory of more than one kind of instruments. It would be noticed, therefore, that the term "accessories" is used in the schedules to describe them which may be manufactured for using as an addition or addition.[562 D F] (5) The fact that they are known as "cInema car bons" does not acquire the character of "agricultural machinery or implement" merely because when used on agricultural land it is also used to draw certain agricultural implements like a plough, sound recording, and sound entry No 11 for dictapsaphone and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and Entry No 11. [563 G H] (6) The use of these words in the Schedules to describe "electrode" to describe those goods which might have been used as an ancillary or supplementary or secondary importance, is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This view was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the High Court that the goods under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No., 4. [564 B C].

The petitioners, who were lessees of a quarry lease granted under the Rules to extract and remove sand from the specified area within their jurisdiction in accordance with the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said rules on various grounds: (1) that the royalty levied by the State Government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose; (2) that there was a reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the impugned notification; and (3) that in the absence of such classification, the levy was invalid. The State Government contended that the said tax should be used either for development or for other pur pose by the Central Government for any of the purposes to which its executive powers extend subject to any law made by the state Legislature on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under article 304(b) applies. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is validly imposed. It is not an imposition made by a law madeby the State Legislature on whom alone the restrictions are in the nature of subordi nate legislation and development and conservation of minerals. It was equally clear that while levying a tax the authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make rules equi lar with any law, rule or those who are placed outside the said rule; and that there is a reasonable connection between the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who were placed outside it. [408C D] 2. The impugned notification in question was made for purposes afor dering the policy of the Act under which the Rules were made for pur pose of regulation and development of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the same tax should he used only as for development of mineral and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. [414D E] 3. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals but while performing its functions pertaining to development if the state incidentally allows extraction to be carry on in public interest, and levies therein are in nature of a fee which could be used exclusively for specific purposes.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the respondent Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. The appellant filed a suit for setting aside the order of the second respondent, the Deputy Commissioner holding that the trusteeship of the temple was "hereditary". The trial court held that the appellant was not hereditary and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of the trustee in the temple of the deceased Kumar Koil was not a hereditary one and that the suit could not be barred by time. HELD: The appellant was hereditary within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. [426 C] The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 (9) is identical in both the Acts. The artificial definition of "succession" in relation to property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". In Re Hindu Women 's Right to Property Act, 1941, it was held that where succession to mahantship is by nomination by the holder in office, it is not a dead succession. The possibility of A being the successor himself is not merely an anomaly, it Is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. There need be no blood relationship between the deceased and his successor but the right of the latter should not depend upon the choice of any individual. [427 D E] In re Hindu Women"s Right To Property Act 1941, (1) A. 448, referred to.

The appellant was charged under section 302/34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The Sessions Court acquitted him of the charge but convicted him under section 201 I. P.C., and sentenced him to death on appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant; (ii) the High court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4 which was corroborated by the contents of the FIR, and (iii) the Sessions Court erred in convicting him on the sole testimony of PW4. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered its intrinsic value of the testimony of this solitary eye witness. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the court while appreciating oral testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were only one assailants and yet there was no blood stains on the bench where he fell dead. On the other hand, the statement of PW 3 who arrived at the place of occurrence when he came running to the place where he was sleeping to the scene of occurrence already when he arrived. It is also conceivable that those persons who arrived in the place immediately after the assault were going to lose their life in such a serious charge it is only necessary that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [707C D] 2. The fact that PW 4 was afflicted with the fell of leprosy has absolutely no motive to implicate the first accused. It may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the assailants who might have already escaped. It also stands to reason that those who gathered at the scene were not and "none of them asked him as to how it had happened". [708E F] 3. The evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 is corroborated by their version in the FIR. The first information report was true that the deceased chased the accused as he was running away after assault. It would have expected some evidence of a trail of blood stains from the place when he fell. It was also conceivable, those persons, who arrived there at the time of lodging the first information Report, were not examined by the prosecution. [808F G] 4. The statement of PWs 2 and3 is corroborated in the F.I.R. lodged at the Police Station which is very close to the spot where he fallen dead. It appears that some persons who gathered there at a little later for information with regard to the assailants, were also not examined. [777G H] 5. The prosecution has made a correct approach in assessing the quality of testimony of PWs 4 and 4. If the statement is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at place of the occurrence already which already stood contradicted by the medical evi dence on a very material point. For the reasons given above, it is difficult to appreciate that he was absolutely reliable there can be no infirmity in convicting the accused.

The assessee was a firm of solicitors. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis and the firm kept their accounts on a cash basis. For the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52 and 1952 53 the assessee claimed that the amounts were not income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of Amarchand out of the oldstandings. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount was not taxable and that section 24B had no application to the case. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee could not be made liable to income tax in the assessment year 1950 51 and notices for subsequent years were invalid. On appeal by the assessee, Held, that the Income tax officer was entitled to assess the total income of a deceased person on the amounts received by him before his death and that received by his heirs and legal representatives after their death but in the previous year in which Amarchand died is liable to be assessed to income Tax under section 24 B of the Income Tax Act. The assessee had ordinarily to be a living person and there could be no assessment on a dead person and the assessment was a charge in respect of the income of that previous year and not a charge for in respect Of the income. The legal representatives of Amar Chand were entitled to assessed the total Income of the deceased person as if the legal representatives were the assessee and the amount were liable to tax under section 23B of the Act after his death but before he had furnished a return which they had been required to furnish under the provisions of section 22 or having furnished a statement which the Incometax Officer has reason to believe to be incorrect, incomplete or incomplete then the Income Incometax Officer can make assessment on the total incomes of the assessee as measured by the income tax of the previous years.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All non domicile employees so relieved shall be provided employment in the Andhra region without break in service and by creating supernumerary posts, if necessary. These supernumerary posts were to be treated as temporary addition to the strength of the office concerned and were to remain adjusted against future vacancies in corresponding posts as they arose. The action was based upon section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act 1957 which was an Act of Parliament made in pursuance of cl. (3) of article 16 of the Constitution making special provision for requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment. The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the constitutional validity of section 3 on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 16(3) provides that ware shall be in India equal to equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or employment to any office under the late. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that article 12. The clause thus enables Parliament to make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement as residence within a State orUnion territory prior thereto. The legislative power to create residential qualification for employment is thus exclusively conferred on Parliament and Parliament can make any law which prescribes any requirement not as to resident within the State or any particular part of it. (ii) Article 15 speaks of residence in a State and only means that that. If it chose to speak of residence outside parts of the State as such Districts, talauqas, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used as such 'any requirement as t residence within the state or Union Territory prior to appointment or employment. (iii) Article 17 speaks of residential qualification in a particular part or State. Having used the word State, the unit is only meant and not any part thereof. The exception, therefore, must be viewed liberally and not carried to excess by interpretation. (iv) The word "State" in article 12 means and includes within its ambit not only the Union territory but also the Union territories which are within the Union Territory of India.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was prosecuted for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and section 5(VI) of the Act, 1898, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had secreted the five registered letters in question and that the almirah was in his exclusive possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father, and that there was no evidence that they were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. HELD : (i) The High court has chosen to accept the evidence of the prosecution with regard to the fact of seizure and that being a question to be decided only by the Court of fact, this Court would not re examine the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the High Court. [416 D] (ii) The appellant was entitled to have some motive for secreting and concealing the registered letter in question. He had no opportunity to get at the articles and he could not be said to have secreted them from the mere fact that they belonged to his father. [418 E F] (iii) The presumption under section 55 of the Evidence Act is that the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence, the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If therefore it was the intention of the legislature that for an officer of the post office to be punished for secreted, destroying or throwing away a postal article in the ocrse of postal articles by an officer appointed even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the articles were riot with which he is required or is competent to deal in the course of his duties. [414 G H] (iv) The fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal Article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal Articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees.

The appellant, a Sarpanch of the Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas, District Deoria, was alleged to have been abused and be laboured and his property worth Rs. 40/ damaged. The Gram Panchayat filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayats, Jankha Khas District Deoria alleging that he had been abused by the appellant and be pleasedoured and be Laboured and that his property valued at Rs.40/ damaged was damaged. On September 10, 1963, the Nyaya panchayat assembled and evidence was led before it. The case was adjourned to December 25, 1963 for a day and hearing the case on December 25. 1963. On December 25 the Nyaya panchayats moved an application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, to transfer the proceedings on the ground that the complainant Yashoda was father of Bunna Prasad Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat Jokhas Khas. The Magistrate rejected this application and directed the Gram Panchayat to postpone the proceedings pending before the Kshettra Panchayat. An urgent copy of the order was applied for and obtained on that very day and the counsel sent a telegram in the following words "Allahabad": "I am not getting any hearing there, and when an application is made there is no hearing there. " The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Magistrate. The High Court held that the five appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that the judicial officer had knowledge of the orders of the High court dated December 20, 1963. [117 D] (2) In certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Court. It must also be borne in mind that Panchas are not well versed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts. [118 E] (3) The order of committal for breach of a prohibitive order is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary finding of a judicial Officer guilty of contempt of court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the Judicial officer had notice of the Order of the high court.

The appellant was tried for the offence of murder and was convicted under section 302, I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah. The High Court dismissed his appeal and confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at the Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appel lant to a police officer and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court were fully established. HELD: The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. Extra judicial confessions arc not usually consider with favour But that does Not mean that the confession coming form a person which has no reasons to state fully and to go to the Police station and report about it. It is always difficult to find reasons for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may be that having blurted out the truth to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appellant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the police Station and report the matter there. [209 C D] The extrajudicial confession of a co accused to Ujagar singh is fully established by the evidence of the eye witnesses whose testimony has been rightly accepted. It cannot therefore be said that the appellant did commit the murder of Sheo Sahai or not, as he had no reason for it to state specifically and to which it was made in circum stances which tendto support his confession.

The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll, the calendar events and the declaration of results of the election. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the notice, and that the declaration was not liable to be quashed. The appellants filed an appeal against the order passed by the High court on January 20, 1979. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals holding that there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition till December 28, 1978 and that as the petitioners were not given any opportunity of being heard before the date fixed for filing the writ petition, they could have filed an application under Rule 6 of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules, 1963. The appeals were dismissed by a Division Bench on January 21, 1979 holding that it was only on December 5, 1978 that the objections and objections received beyond the prescribed period would be considered. On December 31, 1978, the Single Judge issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of election under Rule 46 of the rules pending disposal of the petition. The respondents filed their counter affidavits in support of their claim and contended that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in the notices issued under rule 4(i) of Rules granting 20 days ' time to prefer claims and objection if it had been brought to their notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petitions holding (1) that there is no satisfactory reason for the inordinate delay involved in presentation of the writ peti tion, and (2) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 preferred any claim or objection after October 19, 1978 to the inclusion of an additional prayer that no person preferred any claims or objections after October 20, 1978. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant company was prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for breach of sections 32 and 131 of that Act. The complaint filed against it was dismissed by the Presidency Magistrate. On appeal the High Court held that the company had not been called upon to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not be laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that even in a prosecution under section 134 of the 1913 Act the obligation to send a copy of the balance sheets and profit & loss account is dependent entirely on its being laid before the general meeting of the company. [414 B] In re Varaszha Rao, ; , referred to. The High Courts and the absence of a decision of this Court on section 134 did not refer to the wording of the section but merely stated that the provisions of section 134 were not complied with. It was clear from the provisions under sub section (2) of section 133 that if the balance Sheets were not adopted at the general meetings before which it is laid, a statement of fact and of the reasons therefore had to be annexed to the balance Sheet and profit loss account before an annual general meeting could be held. [416 D E] In the present case the obligation was independent of the holding of the general general meeting and the appellant company had failed to lay before the General body meeting. The failure to reach any one of the stages within the time prescribed was made penal by the Act.

The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum. The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with several offences alleged tending to have committed by them in the way of their search as an assembly armed gang. The trial court acquitted all the accused but convicted them under section 5(1) read with section 5 (2) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. On appeal the High Court quashed the conviction and sentenced the respondent to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which he was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal. Held, that the provisions of section 5 of the Act were not ultra vires the Constitution as they purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not. The classification must not be arbitrary but must be rational, that is to say, it must not only be based on some quali ties or characteristics which are to be found in all the persons grouped together and not in others who are left out but those qualities or qualities must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The distinction between cases where the law does not lay down a standard or form in accordance with which the classification is to be made, it would be the duty of the officers entrusted with the execution of the law to make the classification in the manner they are considered necessary and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases for, in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of offences from another offence or class of cases from another offences or class o fences.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He did not appear for the interview but was also actively associated with teaching under graduate and post graduate students. The appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of Radiology (ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Maulana Gandhi Azad Medical college. On August 19/20, 1968 the Principal, Maulana Nehru Medical College addressed a letter to the appellant conveying that the Vice Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers had granted him recognition as an Associate Professor of radiology (Ex officio) in the Maheed Azad Medical Colleges and treated as an Assistant Professor of Biography (exminence) both from the University. The letter stated that the post was vacant for a period of six years and that the appellant was not holding the post on ad hoc basis. On September 19, 1968, the Principal wrote to the Appellant conveying that he could not be considered for appointment to the post as Associate Professor in the concerned speciality. The Government of India, Ministry of Health & Family Planning, Department of Health and Family Planning issued a letter dated January 17, 1976 stating that the University could not appoint the appellant as Associate professor of Radiologist (exinterested) in Maheed Nehru Medical college since October 9, 1964. By another notification dated January 1, 1965 the initial appointments were notified. The essential pre condition for inclusion of a post in the Central Health Service was that a medical qualification recognised under the Indian Medical Council should be prescribed for it. By the Central Government heath Service (Amendment) Rules 1966, the Central health Service was reorganised with effect from September 9, 1966 and the concept of General Duty officers and Specialist Grade Officers in the service was divided into two classes viz., Class I and Class II. The rules envisaged categorization of personnel manning the service into five different categories viz. Class I & Class II and Class 11. Rule 5 provided for the future maintenance of the Service. 80% of the vacancies therein were to be filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule. Rule 6 provided for appointment of Assistant Professors and Assistant Professor in a teaching hospital attached to the Mawaja Azad Medical University. By a notification dated February 1, 1966 the initial appointment was notified. In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution, the President on May 1, 1963 made the CentralHealth Service Rules, 1963 which came into force on 18th May, 1963. Rule 7 provided for recruitment in accordance with the Second schedule through the Union Public Service Commission subject to the exception made in r.8(2A) with regard to Associate Professors and Assistants. The said rule was further amended by a notification issued on January 1. 1965. By this amendment the Central Medical Health Service Rules were reorganised. Rule 8 provided for initial appointment of Professor or Assistant Professor. In the writ petition filed by the appellant, it was contended that since the post in question was not promotional to the degree of Associate Professor, it could not he considered for selection to the said post as Assistant Professor and that since there was denial of equal opportunity, it would be inappropriate to appoint him on his own post or to make appointment to that post. The High Court dismissed the writ application. In appeal to this Court it was urged that the designation of the appellant in the super time scale was a teaching post and that he had the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the posts of Radiologists cum Associate Professor. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the petitioner as Assistant Professors is a teaching job.

The workmen of the appellant company were referred by the State Government under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items of dispute. The workmen raised a preliminary objection that the Tribunal was not justified in making the calculation of the minimum wage and that it should have been made variable with the Price Index instead of permitting neutralisation to the extent of at least 90%, which could have been done when fixing the minimum wages for the owest, class of workmen. The tribunal rejected this contention on the ground that the other break ups urged on behalf of the workmen were not comparable with the Company and that the evidence was led to show that these concerns were not similar with the company. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the principle for fixation of minimum wages is laid down by this Court in the case of French Motor Co. Ltd., Dwarka Cement Works, Dwarka Cement works, Dwarka cement Works, vs Its Workmen and Another ; , followed. The principle for fixing the Minimum wage primarily on the basis of comparison between different industries in the region is fully justified. It is not necessary that the minimum Wage should be fixed by the tribunal which is being varied by this court in the present case. The Industrial Tribunal has the discretion, in appropriate cases, of making a direction linking the dearness allowance element of a wage to the Price index and leaving the labour to raise a fresh demand and if necessary, a fresh industrial dispute for further rise in wages, in case there is marked variation in the Price List and the wage fixed by it. The Full Bench Formula approved by this decision was not applicable to the present appeal.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was carrying on business under the Railways as well as the Government. The assessee 's total income was assessed at Rs. 69,886/ . On June 3, 1966, the 1st respondent issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961, to the assessee for the assessment year 1960 61. The notice was served on the assessee on June 3 and 1966. In that statement it gave the lull names and address of the alleged creditors. After enquiry, the assessee ' s total income assessed at RS. 69/86 was assessed by the Income Tax Officer under section 147 of the Act. The 1st Respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice as well. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Indian Income tax, 1961. HELD : (i) There is a case for investigating as to the truth of the transactions to which he are not referred in the report. The material that he had before him for issuing notice under s 148 is not mentioned in the Report. In his report the Income 'tax Officer does not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion on the material before him that this is a fit case to issue notice under Section 148. [447C D] (ii) The material which he had to do was that he did not record himself that he was satisfied that by reason of the assessee failing to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting year in question, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. Nor could it be said that he as a consequence of information in his possession, had reasons to believe that the income chargeable under section I.P.C. escaped assessment. [427E] (iii) The important safeguards provided in sections 147 and 151 were lightly treated by the Incometax Officer as well by the Commissioner. Both of them appear to have taken the duty imposed on them under those provisions as of little importance. They had substituted the form for the substance.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calicut, having branches at Madras and Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50 under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. The appellant then moved the High Court under section 66 (2) of 'the Act and the High court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 26 (4). On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that only the terms on which the business under the document of December 6, 1918 was carried on by a person different from those who carried it on in April 1, 1939 and which business had been charged to tax under the Act of 1918 were being carried on at the commencement of the Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the business must have been charged under the Indian income tax Act 1918. [117 E] The fact that the soap business was not even in contemplation, much less in existence before 1922 and the same is true of the umbrella business also shows that the original business in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25 (4) had been rendered applicable. There could be no question of succession to the business carried on in Cal Cochin because the appellant could not be said to have ceased. [118 E] In the present case there was a succession to one of such partnership or not, for the purpose of section 26(2). But it must be remembered that under section 2 (4), a mere change in the constitution of a partnership does not count and sections 25 (1) and 26 (2).

The appellant, who was the plaintiff and his five children, filed a suit for partition of their joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7/24th share. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court has based itself on the judgment in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 394, which had already been overruled and dissented from earlier Division Bench in Rangabai Lalji vs Vasantlal Lalji, A.I.R., 1975 Bom. 257; (ii) the decision of the High court that the properties belonged only to the Joint family was erroneous because Shiramabai, who had partitioned them during his lifetime, had given directions for disposal of the share which was reserved by him for himself in the earlier partitions and therefore, by reason of the provisions of section 8(a) read with the 1st clause of section 9, they took simultaneously and to the exclusion of other heirs. HELD: (i)(i) The Explanation I to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is intended to be explanatory of the provi sions contained in the section, which provides that any property possessed by a female relative specified in that class who claims through such a female heir, the interest of the deceased in the coparcenary property would devolve according to the proviso. Nothing contained in this section shall be construed as enabling a person who has separated himself from the coparcenary before his death. One must imagine a state of affairs which a little prior to Khandappa 's death, a partition of the coparcenary properties was effected between him and other members of the family. The Explanation 1 is intended for explanatory of this provision. [766 B C] (ii)(a) It is not necessary that there should be a notice under section 22 and its non compliance with it.

The appellant Corporation was incorporated in the year 1960. The age of retirement of its employees was 58 years. In 1959, there were more than 200 insurers carrying on life insurance business in India. As it came to notice of the Government that the Indian Life Insur ties (Staff) Regulations, 1960, were being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management, the Corporation decided to nationalise the life insurance busi ness. Pursuant to the said decision, the President promulgated the Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956, which provided for vesting of the management of the life Insurance business in all the insurers in India by an order made by the Central Govern ment under section 11(2) of the Act. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of regulation 19(2), on the ground that it was violative of article 14 and 16 of the Constitution, as it had not been passed after 1st September 1956, and that the regulations were made in contravention of the provisions of the Life Institu ties Act, 1951. The High Court held that the employees of the Corporation after it was estab lished, i.e., after 1 st September 1956 and the transferred employees insofar as the age of superannuation was concerned, had been given retrospective effect from 20th June 1979, and accordingly quashed the regulation 19 (2) on the grounds that the employee of the Corpora tion was not in terms applicable to the transferred employee who became the employees under sub section (1) of section 11 of the , and only referred to the employees and agents of the Corpo ration who were employed after 1th September 1956. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had the right to continue in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age Of 60 years as a Class III employee, the distinction between an employee who entered the service of the corporation after it is establi lished i. e., after Ist September 1956 was raised to 60 years and that therefore, the respondent was not entitled to continue his services beyond the age 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post or Class II post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conditions of service of employees were regulated by the provisions Of the Life insurance (Efforts) Regulations 1960 as amended in 1976 and the regulations made under clause (bb) of sub section(2 of section 49(2).

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice of India and the Prime Ministers. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. The appellants were informed that Justice D.S. Tewatia had visited the Bar and inspected the Court at Charkhikot on 17 2 1975. The Chief Justice, however, did not see the Chief Justice and left the letter with the Registrar in a closed cover addressed to him for being handed over to him. The Registrar told them that the closed cover could reach the Hon 'ble Chief Justice on 17 3 1975. In the meanwhile, the Chief Minister of Haryana wrote a communication to the Chief justice of India requesting him to take appropriate action in this regard. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of Bar Association. The contempt proceedings were dropped. The appellant filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for its acceptance of his apology and for the same relief. The Single Judge who heard the matter, held that the letter was not a scandalising the Honble Judge or the Chief Justices of Punjab and Haryana and dismissed the contempt petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contents of the letter which he addressed to others and criticises the views expressed by him were correct; that the High court proceeded on the basis that the letters written by the appellants were correct, that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The letters written at the back of the appellant and said "on a perusal of the contents thereof a prima facie case contempt is made out. It is no part of duty of a Judge nor is it a duty of the Judge nor was it a Duty of a judge nor is he it aduty of a Court in discharge of his office of a Judges. [246C D] 2. The statement that the Judges were told to believe that a Judge ought always to steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters, or to concern themselves with political issues or policies taken by political parties as a part of their political programme, cannot be construed as scandalising or defiling the Hon"ble Judge nor can it be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of court. [245D] 3. The apology tendered on behalf Of some organisa tion is not a conditional apology. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communica tion in question constituted for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tenders his apology to this Hon 'leble Court for the said purpose and prays for its rejection. [247E F] 4. The allegation in the letters was not disputed. It appears that the appellants committed no contempt of the court there was never any occasion for acceptance of apology. In view of this, it is not possible to say that the matters did not constitute contempt. [248F G] 5. The allegations in letter were against the appellant. The contents thereof are of opinion that the matter did not constituted contempt. The Judges are by reason of their office and nature of work expected not to get involved in controversial matter, or political issues. Invitations by the Bar Associations of Charhi Dadri and communal parochial lines. Invitingitations by Public discussion on political matters or policies under taken by local parties as part of its political programme. [249A B] 6. The Judge travels from his judicial work and descends into the arena of politics and parties. The judge cannot in such a case take shelter behind his office if the public discusses and criticise the views spoken by him. [250C D, G] 7.

The petitioner, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, was carrying on business in cloth. It had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded taxa tion. The petitioner claimed that the provisions of sections 5(1), 5(4) and 6 of the Act were ultra vires as they infringed article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that section 5(5) of the impugned Act was void as it contravened articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion and was void under article 14 Of the Constitution and was thus void and unenforceable. The provisions of section 5 (1) and (6) were not ultra vires article 14. The procedure prescribed by the impugned law in sections 6 and 7 was more drastic than the procedure prescribed in sections 37 and 38 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and those dealt with under section 34 of the said Act and those dealing with all persons who evade payment of income tax and came within the ambit of section 34. The impugned Act did not contravene article 14 or 19 of that Constitution. The provision for investigation into the validity of the provisions Of sections 5 and 6 was more stringent than the prescribed procedure in sections 38 and 38. The classification made by the Commission under the provisions was reasonable and conclusive and could not be challenged as violative of articles 14, 19 and 31 of the constitution. Held further, that the impugned section did not offend article 14 nor was it invalid. The Act was a valid piece of discriminatory legislation and was therefore void. The restrictions imposed by section 5 were reasonable and in the interest of the general public and were reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 19(6) Of the Constitu tution. The object of the , namely, to prevent evasion or evasion of income Tax was not to prevent or delay evasion of tax but to prevent avoidance or evasion. The power conferred on the Commission by section 6(5), therefore, must be exercised in a reasonable manner and not arbitrarily.

The appellant Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Respondent No. 1) is a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops ,and Establishments Act, 1954. The primary objects of the Federation are to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport, industry and manufacture, finance and all other economic subjects and to secure the services of expert technical and other men to secure services of experts (vide clauses (f) and (k) of Memorandum of Association). It undertakes regular publication of periodicals, bulletins etc. for the benefit of businessmen, industrialists and industrialists by securing them for the services Of expert technical men (vide clause (h) of memorandum of Association) and also undertakes regular public publication of annuals, fireins etc., for the benefits of technical experts (Vide clauses (g) and(k)of Memorandum of association. It undertakes periodical publication of quarterlys, calins etc.; to promote industrial and commercial pursuits; to provide for arbitration in respect of disputes arising in the course of trade, industry or other business matters. The appellant Federation filed a writ petition before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order passed by the Chief Inspector (Appellant) on February 4, 1964. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the premises of the appellant Federation were not a commercial establishment within the definition of "commercial Establishment" given in section 2 (9) of Delhi Shops Act, and that the activities carried on in the premises amounted to "work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto". In appeal by certificate the appellant contended: (1) The advice in question was not tendered for any consideration; (2) The letter dated February 4. 1964 issued by the appellant was never received by it; (3) The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section II(9) and that its activity amounted to a 'profession ' within the term of section 3(5); (4) The Association failed to pay the admission fee of Rs. 1,000/; (5) The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments, Delhi (Appellant 2 herein) called upon the Federation to register its establishment under the Act; (6) The Union did not comply with this direction and urged that it had not been an "industry" as contemplated in section 3 (9); (7) The appellant should not be allowed to commit a volte face and take up in this Court a stand which was either not taken or was given in no. the High court; (8) The question whether the activity of the Union partakes the character of trade or business is essentially a charitable organisation and not a professional one. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of 'commercial establishment ' given in the Act includes a "shop" and commercial establishment. [352E] 1.2 The definition is wide enough to include within its ambit all the property and income of the association. The very definition of the expression "commercial establishments" indicates that the activity, of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried on by it amounts to a busi (i) any trade, business or profession; (ii) any work in connection therewith or incidental thereto is carried on. There is no doubt that the registered office of the Association is one of general utility; the only source of its income is from subscriptions. The occasional exhibitions or museums organised by it are activities which are only incidental or subsidiary to the primary charitable object of theAssociation. It takes up with the specific difficulties experienced by the trade in the day today business and endeavours to attain for the traders and industrialist by securing their services of technical expert men (Vide clause (f), (k).

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his descendants. During the previous year of assessment years 1949 50, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ on account of the aforesaid pension. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that the sum of RS. 36.396/ was chargeable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) that an annuity is not always taxable as income. The remuneration not being received as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income is received, it is not exempt under section 4(3)(viii). (ii)that the allowance varied from year to year and was merely a measure, indicated the source of that right in lieu of which the allowance was given. The source of an allowance or pension is the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is income. (iii)The payment of the "pension" in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assesse 's predecessor in 1838 is not a capital receipt and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion, one permit to the Karnataka state Tourism Development corporation and another permit to be granted by the Karnataka Government. The State Road transport Corporation, which was a nationalised State Undertaking, had granted 11 out of eleven permits to its Karnataka State Transport Corporation and the other private operators. The Karnataka State Tourist Development Corporation, however, granted 11 more permits to private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Tamil Nadu State Tourism Corporation. The appellant State Road Road Transport Corpora ties challenged the grant of 12 out of nine permits to it by way of writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63(7) contemplated exclusion of the 'non preferred category ', if sufficient number of applicants from the ' non preferred classes were available. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Karnataka Road Transport Corp., it was contended that (i) the preference envisaged by the Proviso to section 64(7), the application from the "non preferred" category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from the applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number; (ii) the fourth sub clause of the proviso thereto offended article 14 and had to he struck down. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The scheme excludes omnibus operators and requires applicants to have two years experience in the car hire business or that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies either of indigenous taxies of either indigenous or make acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the vehicle hire business. [1016B] 2. The proviso to s 63( 7) does not expressly refer to "other things being equal". It is clear that while considering the application for stage carriage permit under section 47, the private operator has an equal chance to get a permit even on inter State route if it shows that the Undertaking is either unable to provide efficient and economical service or that the private operators are better equipped to render the same. Preference in this context would mean that other things generally appearing to be qualitatively and quantitatively, though equal, the application of the Undertaking shall be given priority over other applicants. [1065D E] 3. The Scheme excludes omnibus operator and requires applications to have one year experience in a car hire service business or to own five tourist taxis. There are no guidelines as to how the discretion to grant approval is to be exercised once the minimum conditions are fulfilled. [ 1016C D] 4. The object of the Proviso is to enable the State Transport Undertaking to reserve certain percentage of stage carriage permits for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Section 47(1) provides that other matters being equal, a registered cooperative society and a person possessing a licence for driving transport vehicles shall be give preference over applicants in granting stage carriage Permits. [1006E] 5. The general scheme excludes operators and require applicants to had sufficient contacts with travel agencies hoteliers/apartments, etc. and should have sufficient contact with travel agency agencies hoggoteliers or a tourist taxi ties. There were no guidelines which the discretion was to be applied once the conditions are satisfied. [10016G] 6.

HELD: The High court has no authority under section 19(2)(c) of Act to frame the impugned rule. [663 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , applied. In Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, A.I .R. 1959 Mad. 816, referred to. The appellant was appointed as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison. On March 25, 1954 he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant. In substance the charges were that while he was serving at Surendranagar District Jail he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The appellant filed a written statement on September 4, 1954, and an enquiry was held by Mr. Gangopadhyay. He was dismissed by the Inspector General of Prisons. On appeal the District Judge confirmed the order of dismissal but the High Court in revision held that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that (i) the High court erred in holding that there has been a violation of article 31(2); (ii) the order passed by the lower appellate court was not liable to be set aside because (a) the Government servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the report of the Enquiry Officer; and (b) the finding on the basis of the enquiry held against him was based upon tort but was a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a). HELD : The decree of the High ' Court decreeing arrears of salary is truly a liability. In proceedings relating, to a Contract within section 30(2), the judgment of the trial court decreeing payment of arrears of pay is truly an " liability in proceeding relating to contract within Section 60(1) (a). It is true that the question whether reasonable opportunity has or not been afforded to the Government servants must depend on the facts of each case but it would be in very rare cases indeed in which it could be said that the Government Servant is not prejudiced. The words "actionable wrong other than breach of contract" in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of salaries, the decree properly falls under section 60 of the Act rather than under section 61. [922 C D] The High Court was right in holding the appellant guilty of tort because the order was not passed by it and the finding was against him. If the report was against the appellant he would have utilised its reasoning to dissuade the InspectorGeneral from coming to a contrary conclusion, and if the report were against him he would be able to put such arguments or material as he could dissuade the inspector General from accepting the report. [ 923 A B] The decree passed by this Court in State of Tripura vs The Province of East Bengal, ; , applied.

The appellant 's land was leased to one M.M. Mathews, who had granted a lease of the same land in favour of M. Mathew. The respondents were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama Collieries Ltd., and the appellant leased out the said land to M. M.Mathew. On August 2,1900, the appellant granted a mining lease of certain coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of the rest of the encroached portion. The appellant 'land was situated immediately to the south of the respondents ' land. On September 2, 1901, the respondents filed an application for the issue of a permanent injunction restraining them from encroaching upon the appellants ' coal and cutting and removing coal therefrom. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the respondents had encroached upon the appellant ' land and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court on appeal held that the respondent had encroached on the appellant land, that the lease was not barred by limitations and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. On appeal by certificate: Held, that in view of the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below, the finding of fact must be affirmed. The onus is upon the plaintiff to prove that he had knowledge of the encroachment only within three years of the date of the filing of the suit and that he failed to discharge that burden. The respondent was not entitled to rely on any evidence which had the effect of shifting the onus of proof to establish his case. The mere fact that the appellant had encroached into a portion of its coal mines did not by itself prove that the encroachment was prior to 1932, but there is no acceptable evidence on record to show that the encroached area was entirely lost to them for ever. In the present case the respondents were using the land for mining purposes and they had absolutely no knowledge or information whatsoever regarding it. The question whether they had adduced evidence which they had failed to prove was not raised either before the Subordinate Judge or before the High Court. Nor could they hold in favour Of the appellant on the basis of such a possibility.

The appellant was a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter and he abused the Engineer, Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold by other workmen and taken outside. It was alleged that the appellant had resorted to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders. The tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21, 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The appellant could not therefore be allowed to contend that he was entitled under r, 18 (b) of Standing Orders to dispense with the service of any employee at any time by giving 14 days notice or paying 12 days wages. The question whether the employer could defend the action under r., 18(a) was a matter which had to be decided on evidence and not by the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Court in the present case had jurisdiction, as it was exercising its power under that rule, to interfere with such termination of service even though it was satisfied that the action taken under the rule was colourable exercise of power. The decision of this Court in Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, ; , relied on. Parshotham Lal Dhingra 's Union vs Union, [1952] S.C.R. 869, followed.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for declaration that they were entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre, and for an injunction restraining the defendants from interfering directly or indirectly with its rights to obtain the cinema films. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the issues were not purely of law, that in any event the case or any part thereof was not likely to be disposed of on these issues, and that ordinarily in "appealable cases" the Court should, as far as possible decide all the issues together and that piecemeal trial might result in protracting the litigation. The High Court also rejected the contention that there was no bar of estoppel, and held that evidence as to the true nature of the transaction was not inadmissible by virtue of section 92 of the Evidence Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the trial court had decided the question of res judicata in a suit without recording evidence; (ii) the issue asked for in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses could form the subject matter of an issue, and (iii) the High court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issues. HELD : (i)(a) The order passed by the High Courts was set aside and the Trial Court was directed to proceed with the trial. [439 C] (b) The question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated December 1, 1960 was in the nature of a lease or other character had to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent decree of December 1.1960, could not operate as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit which is superadded the seal of the Court. A matter in controversy in an action may operate as a bar of resjudicata only if there is an adjudication by the court; the terms of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure are substantially subject to three important conditions (1) that the decision is of a Court subordinate to the High ,Court, and in which no appeal lies. [442 E F] (2) that there is a case which has been decided by the subordinate Court; and (3) that it was for the Trial court in the first instance to decide that question and allow the whole question, that was once closed for all by consent of decree of 12 1 1960. But the only thing that can be said is so that far as the agreement of November 27, 1954 created a lease, the consent decree must be held to create a bar in res judicata.
