However, the 'Formula of a 'eemula of substantial and compelling reason ' must be left out of account. To entitle an accused person to claim the benefit of any doubt, the benefit must be reasonable even as any doubt the benefit is of some doubt,the benefit of which an accused may claim must be reasonably as nearly probable as that against him.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court was convicted by the Madras High Court under section 5(2) read with article 124(5) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 161 or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to try the case and that the order of removal was imperative under clause (4) of Article 124 read with Article 2 18 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that: (1) the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the High Court or of the State Government from his office though the Presi dent appoints the Judge by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the States as he may deem necessary for that purpose and in case of the appointment of a Judge other than the Chief justice of the Madras Supreme Court and of the high Court by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith the Chief Justices of such Judges of the said High Court and the Supreme court; (2) the requirement of previous sanction under section 6 for prosecution of a judge of the Bombay High Court is the authority competent to remove him from office without any cause being shown or incapacity; (3) the fact that the accused person or any other person on his behalf is in possession, for which the public servant cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income for which he cannot satisfactorily Account, of financial resources or properties disproportionate to the known sources, of income, would not be a valid ground for granting sanction under Section 6; (4), even if the holder of a public office during his tenure in office is in pos session for which such public servant can satisfactorily account of pecuniary assets or resources disproportionate to him known sources Of income, he cannot successfully account of such pecuniary resources and property disproportionate by his known source of income. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of clause (c) of Section 5(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act,1947 are not intended to be covered by the Act.

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Castes. He challenged the election on various grounds, inter alia, on the ground that he did not belong to any Scheduled Caste within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the expression "excluding Saha" in item 40 meant excluding Sahas from Sunri caste and they had been specifically excluded in item 41 for greater safety o f the Sunri. HELD: (i) The word 'included ' in item 39 means excluding Saha ' in the item. Therefore, when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste, the other must be a caste. [391 D] (ii) In the absence of such words "grains" in the entry, it would have been so read that the word ' Saha excluding those who bore the surname Saha ' meant excluding those whose names had not been included in the Scheduled Caste. That is why the Tribunal went wrong in interpreting item 40 in the light of the evidence before it. [390 E] (iii) The words "parts or groups" in article 341 were wide enough to refer to any determinate part of a caste distinguished by a surname or otherwise and it was not necessary that such part must necessarily form a sub caste. It follows that when the item excluded Sahas in the expression 'excluding Saha ', in the Item must, without more refer to a caste group within the Sunrri caste, be equally another caste group.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was arranged that the complainant should bring with him Rs. 1,000 for the articles of furniture (Exhibit E) a letter to the Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Committee for transfer of the telephone connection to the appellant 's name and address. The appellant and his wife were leaving the flat, the man who masaded as the complain ant 's brother threw off his disguise and disclosed their identity. The police party, who was down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers that were handed over to him by the appellant. The Presidency Magistrate convicted the appellant under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a part of the rent from the respondent. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held, that the word "relinquishment" in section 19 (1) of 'the Act means "a relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises". The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of his rights as such. Whether abandonment of a lease would come within the meaning of section 19 sub clause (i), of the Transfer of Property Act, would have been more appropriate. Section 15 and 18 of the Act were referred to in this connection but in the present case there was no "relation" within the definition of art and was used in the Transfer Of Property Act. The distinction between an assignment on the one hand and relinquishment or surrender on the other is too plain to be ignored. In the case of an assignment, the assign ment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case Of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not essential, in view of section 18 which speaks of relinquishment of tenancy of premises by a tenant. If, by the expression "an assignment" the transfer of a right by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offence, then the words "the relinquishment of the tenancy of the premises by any tenant" would be more appropriate and would not be less than the sum or value of the consideration received by him.

The Tata Consultant Employees Union, a company, was dissolved and in 1974 the undertaking became one of the divisions of Tata Sons Limited. The workmen served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant, and as their demands were not accepted conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable and on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The award was challenged by the appellant before the Industrial Tribu nal, Maharashtra. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the company 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. The appellant filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance, which was rejected by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that having regard to the financial capacity of the company to bear additional financial onus if the demand was accepted, the Tribunal erred in making the wage scale retrospective and that retrospective effect should be given to the workmen only after the flat increase is added to the present basic salary. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment made by the Industrial Court has the effect of providing a second increase to the pay of each individual workman. [177D] 2. The additional financial liability which the Tribunal was entitled to correct was considered in detail and regard was had to their original structure and the accretions made subsequently by way of dearness allowances and house rent allowance. In view of the revision of wage scales, there would be consequent increase in the dearness allowance and house Rent allowance. [176F] 3. The increase was for a flat increase of Rs. 150/ and again after the figure Rs. 100/ and then after the figures Rs. 50/ and Rs. 200/ respectively. The increased financial burden is added only after flat increase was added to present basic salaries of each employee. [178G H; 178A] 4. The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal also does not reveal that there was any opposition by the company regarding the application for correcting the award so as to bring out what was intended. [179B C] 5. The corrigendum was in effect a fresh award. It is more than plain that the increase was the one incorporated in the revised wage scales pertaining to those categories. The addition was integrated as a feature of the pay scale and the revised pay scales. [180C D] 6. The fact that the Tribunal had fixed the dearness allowances in the light of the award did not indicate that there were any opposition from the company. The direction dated December 21, 1978 made consequent thereto is also quashed.

The appellant, a sugar mill, was awarded wages at the rate of Rs. 2/2 per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. The appellant paid its employees only as their employees. As the agreement did not provide for payment of any wages, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled and could not be included in the main definition of wages under section 2(vi) of the Act. HELD: (i) The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed by an award cannot be treated as wages under s 2(v) of Act. [422 B C] (ii) The fact that references made under section 10(1) of Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have constantly been examined by industrial adjudica tion and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore, the basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad for the appellant that the applications made by the respondents were incompetent under section 15 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1947, was correct.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma and misappropriated the same. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but on appeal the High Court held that the evidence did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the conviction of the appellant was illegal as sanction had not been obtained under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and if sanction was necessary, the prosecution which had resulted in the conviction was initiated without any sanction under section 19(1). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that sanction under s. 197(i) of Cr. P.C. was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409. [167 B] In the present case the elements alleged against the second accused were first, that there was an 'entrustment ' and/or 'd seconded '; second, that the entrustment and/ or 'discount ' was dominion or in the circumstances of the case the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. Clearly, therefore sanction under S. 197 (1) Cr.P.C., could not be prosecuted under section 411, and the absence of such sanction was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. [168 C D] Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1948 P. C. 185, referred to.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in Travancore State. It filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90,947 representing only the profit made by it in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i). The proper function of a proviso is to except and deal with a case which would otherwise fall within the general language of the main enactment, so as to exclude from it by implication what the enactment clearly falls within its express terms. It has to operate in the same field and if the language of a statute is clear and unambiguous, a proviso can have no repercussion on the interpretation of the provisions of the principal enactment so as not to exclude it by necessary implication what clearly falls under its express words. [264 D E] (ii) The proper functioning of a Proviso is that it qualifies the generality of the primary enactment by providing an exception and taking out as it were, from the main provision, by providing something by way of an addendum or dealing with a subject which is foreign to the main Act.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co. was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of which the appellant was a private company. The first respondent was incorporated on January 1946 and its Head Office was at Calcutta. In July 1947 the first respondent 's concern was converted into a Public Limited Company. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age 55. The Tribunal held that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region, there had trend been to fix the age at 60 and not at 55. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal 's finding that in many of the awards the trend had been to fixed the age was not very commendable and that its present conclusion that in several the awards recent trend had to be judged in the light of other material and relevant circumstances, and that one of the important considerations in this connection would be that the age Of retirement can be and often determined on industry cum region basis. Held: (i) The Tribunal was wrong in making those decisions. (ii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very sound. It ought to add in this respect, that the approach adopted in dealingwith this aspect is not quite commendable. (iii) In spite of these infirmities it cannot be said that there was a trend in Bombay Region which had been fixed at 55 or 58. The fact that in some of the concerns the clerical and subordinate staff were not organised into trade unions would not justify any doubt about the correctness of what was said on the earlier occasion. (iv) In view of this Court 's decision in Dunlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, , it is doubtful whether the conclusion recorded by this Court in some Of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in the Bombay region was accurate. Having embarked an enquiry, the Tribunal appears to have taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it has ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend is established in fact.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the offence of dacoity. The trial court acquitted them but the High Court, in appeal, took the view that the presumption under section 41 1.7 of the Indian Penal Code was not drawn as the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution case was not established because dacoity was committed at night and large quantities of stolen goods were found in their houses. HELD : The conviction was correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. [723 B] In what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be drawn under section 114 of the Evidence Act has to be drawn. In what circumstance the one of the presumption or other may he drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reason is obvious. Disposal of the fruit of the crime requires the finding that a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determine whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be draw.

The petitioners are manufacturers of 'thinner ' containing spirit and other ingredients and other soluble material. They were manufacturing only liquid substance, namely, "poisons" which contain only liquid substances. The percentage of such solu ble material does not exceed 30% as poison. The petitioners ' contention that the use of the word "suison" in Rule 2(x)(2) of the Rules is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution was rejected by this Court. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the are invalid and must be declared ultra vires. [225B] 1.2 The provisions are not discriminatory or violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitu tion. They are not hit by any consti tutional limitation. [226D] 2.1 There is no substance in the contention that there was discrimination between the petitioners and the respondents. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. [227D] 1:2 The object of the enactment is to regulate the possession and sale of poisons. Some substances were included in the Rules made in 1926 as poisons and that is not in dispute. Section 4 of the act specifically sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as poison, which destroys living tissues, the substance can be safely called poison. [228E F] 2:3 The nature or character of trade is such as inherently hazardous to health. It may be a deadly poison or a valuable medicine according to how and how much is taken. If the resultant effect of administering into the system pro duces sion thereof desirable, any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison.[228F] 2(i) The object is to regulating the importation, possession and Sale of poison. Some substance which was used for pur pose mentioned therein could definitely be treated as poison by the time or manner of their adminis tration. Nothing is a poison unless regard has to its administration. A substance may be an a deadly medicine or a thing that destroys or fatal changes which destroys live tissues, which destroy living beings, the substances can safely be called poison.[225G H] 3:1 The nature and character of the trade in the poison is not automatically made applicable to the other States. [224A B] 2.(ii) The use of word "poison" as it is used in Rule 1(x) (2) is an extremely dangerous or inherently dangerous condition which cannot be said to have any absolute right. It would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [229D E] 3.1 In the instant case, neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by Article 14.

The assessee firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, mercuries, mercure etc. In the assessment of income tax for the year 1952 53, relevant to the account year 1953 54, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 2,68,385/ as bad debt due from the Bombay firm at the foot of its accounts. The Income tax Officer disallowed this claim on the ground that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as Chemists and Druggists nor in the nature of a loan advanced in the ordinary course of business transactions. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but held that the amount was not one incurred in the business of the assesses, and that the High Court had erred in disallowing the sum claimed by the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the finding reached by the tribunal was not supported by proper discussion of the material before it and that it gave no reasons in support of its conclusions. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the debts were not sent to the Bombay Firm as loans made in the normal course of its money lending business, nor in respect of any other business of assessee. [423 D] The finding with regard to the whole of the amount sought to be deducted is binding on this Court. It is true that the tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that findings reached by it are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assesses to the Madras firm were not loans made, in the regular course of their money lendingbusiness, nor any interest was charged by the appellants in respect thereof.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was brought into force on September 20, 1984. Section 11 A of the Land Acquisition Act provides that where the said declaration has been published before the commencement of the Act, the entire proceedings for acqui sition of the land shall lapse. Under the first proviso to Section 11A it was prescribed that where such a declaration had been made within two years from the date of the publication of the declaration and that if no award is made within that period, the whole proceedings for acquisition of the said lands shall lapse; under the second proviso to the first Proviso to Section II A, the period during which any action or proceeding to be taken in pursuance of the aforesaid declaration was stayed by an order of a Court shall be excluded. The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within the stipulated time. In these two writ petitions, the Karnataka High Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of lands. These appeals were also dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so, his application is liable to be rejected. [567B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the stay orders were highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. The High Court has granted interim order staying further proceedings. Whatever the ultimate effect of the stay order was highly material, the application is not liable to he dismissed.

The appellant bank was employed in banks which were not governed by the provisions of the Sastry Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The award dealt with the method of adjustment in the scales of pay fixed by it from para 5.329 onwards. It divided the employees of the banks with which it was concerned in two groups. The first group consisted of workmen who were drawing basic pay on January 1, 1962 according to scales of Pay provided by that award. In the second group consisted Of workmen who entered service before January 1. 1959 and those who entered Service on or after January 1,. 1959. In both the groups consisted of those who joined service before 1.1.1959 and thosewho entered service on or before January l, 1959. The workman 's basic pay as on January I, 1962 was Rs. 100 as modified. The Sastry Award dealt with method of adjustments in the scale of pay from January 1 to 1962 according as modified and were not thus drawing basic salary on the footing of scales of payment provided by the Sastry award as modified, but were not so drawing basic Pay on the basis of scales fixed by the Desai Award as laid down in Prakash Chand Mehra 's case. The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of the Desai award the adjusted basic pay was to be as on 1st January 1959 and thereafter they would be fitted in the new scales ofpay provided by cl. 329 onwards, and that the adjustment would give him or the maximum in the old scale applicable to them under the Sastry awards. The Labour Appellate tribunal held that the basic pay under cl.(ii) had to be worked out as on December 1, 1959 and therefore it was not a case of revision of basic pay. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that basic pay had to he fixed as on April 1, 1960, and his salary should be fixed at Rs. 182. The Tribunal was wrong in its modification of the award. It is true that there are some verbal changes in the Sastry ' award but these verbal changes are only due to lapse of time and do not affect the substance of what was provided by it as modified; but these changes have been considered necessary having regard to the lapse of the time after coming into force of the provisions Of the Sastry Act. The Award made certain changes and therefore need not be interpreted in the same way as was done in Prakashchand Mehra ' case.

[254E] 4:3.

The respondent assessee, a firm carrying on banking business, had maintained an account in the books of M/s Pearls and Beads. The Income Tax Officer found that the account showed a credit of Rs. 1,50,000 to his son and this amount was validly gifted by him to his sons and grand sons. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee did not validly assign Rs.1,50.000 in favour of his sons, grand sons and hence the amounts had been wrongly included in his net wealth. The Tribunal also held that there was no valid gifts. In the reference under section 27(1) of the Act, the High Court answered the first question in the negative and so far as the second question is concerned it declined to answer the second in the affirmative and so the question for determination in the appeal by special leave was whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal right ly held that gift made by transfer en tries in the book of company company were valid. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in favour the revenue. [131C] 2.1 In the instant case, except to the extent indi cated above, the entries in the account could not effectuate gifts. As the respondent is not appearing there will be no valid gift if sums or funds are not available. It is possible in certain circumstances for a donor to make a valid gift by book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid transfer even though it may have sufficient cash balance but it must have sufficient provision for overdraft with the bank on the basis it could honour the instructions given by the assessee. [132D E] 2:2. The fact that the respondent had made a gift of Rs,50 lakhs to his wife and his wife respectively, would not make any valid gift unless and until such enjoyment or benefit was clearly referable to the gift, i.e., to the gifted, i e. to the entire exclusion of the donor, or to the whole exclusion of that donor in any benefit to him by contract or otherwise. [133E F] 2(a) The High Courts were wrong in answering a question in this manner in the manner it did. [134G] (b) In the case of Chimanbhai Lalbhai vs Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., , the assessee had a substantial credit balance exceeding the sum of Rs 50,000 which he purported to give to his father, more entries in his account in his accounts and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. With effect from 28th March 1957 L was taken as a partner in the firm by giving debit entries in its account in their account and corresponding credit to the account of L. [135E F; 135A] (c) The entries in books of a Banking Company and gifts were held to be valid. In that view of the matter, except for the extent of indi bility or sufficient provision, upon the basis of which it would honour the instruction given by assessee, there was sufficient funds at the disposal of the donee by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries. [136B C] 2.(a) In view of section 123 of the , and the Sale of Goods Act, it is clear that there were sufficient cash balances out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee more entries, more in the accounts, and credited. In case of banking companies or firms, if these companies or firm do not have overdraft facilities, it was not possible to make valid gift, if sums and funds are available. [137C] (d) The fact of gift, it could not be said that the donee had not retained the possession and enjoyment of the property to the exclusion of donor in some benefit to himself by contract etc.

The High Court took a policy decision to the effect that as a general rule, judicial officers working in special posts whether cadre or non cadre outside their regular line should be recalled to the regular line after the completion of three years service. The Government by its letter dated April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three year service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the government was reluctant. Every time the High Court requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district judges or sessions judge and addl. district judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. In the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The High Court was repeatedly requesting the government not to release these officers for being transferred to administrative posts as judges or as addl district judges and addi district judges. The government by its order dated October 10, 1966 directed that the three officials mentioned above be retained for a period of two years or till they were actually holding those posts. On March 6, 1967 a special Bench of the High court took the precipitate step of transferring the aforesaid officers to other posts and in their place officers who were posted as District judges and sessions judge respectively. The State Government by an order dated November 10, 1968 directed that all these officers should be retained in administrative posts till the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Shri P.C. Dey was rendered. On December 10, 1967 the High Courts ordered the following transfers: (a) Shri K.B. Patro, the then law department as deputy secretary to the Government of Orissa, (b) Shri B.K. Patrol, the former law department, a post which was vacant and then then the Law Department; (c) Shri P C Dey, the latter, the Law Secretary and legal remembrancer and the other officers holding the posts of the law secretary, deputy law and the administrative member sales tax tribunal respectively. On January 6, 1968 a special bench of the Orissa High Court passed orders transferring the aforementioned officers to the other posts in the secretariat for assuming charge of the posts to which they were posted. The appellants challenged the order of the Government on the grounds that (1) the High COurt had no authority to hold the posts in question; (2) the government had not followed the principle laid down in that decision and (3) the orders of transfer made by the High Curt were invalid because they had no power to do so. The respondents contended that (i) the Government was competent to institute disciplinary proceedings against an addl District judge and sessions Judge; (ii) the officers included there was the Registrar of the Punjab High Court at the very commencement of his arguments conceded that the order transferring the said officers to another post was not a law secretary but was only an administrative officer. HELD: (1)(a) The High COrt had no jurisdiction to direct the Government to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a judge or to one of the post in secretariat. [156 D] (b). The cadre with which we are concerned is that of the senior judicial service. It is not the case that the appellants were placed at the disposal of the government for any definite period. [157 E F] (c). The High Courts have power to fill those posts by transfer of judicial officers. The executive cannot know the requirements of a particular court, the High Commis sioner and the Government should not forget the fact that powers are conferred on them for the good of the public and they should act in such a way as to advance public interest. If there is mutual understanding and appreciation of the difficulties of one by the other, there will be harmony.

The workmen of the Alembic Glass Industries Ltd. Baroda, and their workmen, who were employed in the factory of the appellant company, claimed that they should be entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness only in the case of a spell of sickness for which no sickness benefit was last paid. The Industrial Tribunal held that the sickness benefits could not be granted retrospectively or allowed to accumulate and that the workmen were entitled to receive more wages by remaining absent than on duty. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award of the Industrial Tribunal and remanded the matter to it with certain directions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) as the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of the Act are already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, they were not entitled to any sickness benefit during the first one of the days of sick leave; (ii) that the benefit under the scheme of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme could not he said to have been denied by the companies in both cases. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal was justified in its view that the workers were entitled for 7 days sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. It would thus appear that the appellants had not been able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [864C D] 2. The Scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave. The scheme of benefits admissible to the workmen in the present case is not similar to those applicable under the Employees State Insurance Act, 1948. [874D E] 3. The appellants have not been unable to show why the awards should not be allowed by other companies in the region. They are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave in addition to 15 days casual leave and pay in lieu of privilege leave. [884E F] 4. The benefits admissible cannot be denied on the ground that it had not be given by other Companies in the State. [851C D; 863A B] 5. The benefit of sick Leave is available only in case of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner.

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the , on a charge of entering India territory without the requisite authority, and was arrested on September 9, 1955. He was taken into custody and interrogated and physically assaulted and threatened with dire consequences. The grounds of detention were vague. The detaining authority, in exercising its power failed to apply its mind to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention. The appellant made his professional assistance to him and obtained an order of release on bail from the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, which was foiled by the police on September 8, 1955, at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor. The High Court directed on March 3, November 1954, the return forthwith of all the papers and articles seized. Held, that the order of detention was mala fide and that it was not necessary to mention particulars of the activities carried on by the detenu or the names of any of the persons aiding him. It is not possible to state affirmatively more on the question of what is vague. It must vary according to the circumstances of each case. The right to be furnished adequate particulars of grounds of detained, to enable a proper representation being made, is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) which implies, the right to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest. The failure to communicate the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation cannot be implied in these circumstances. In the present case there was no substance in the contention that the grounds furnished were not vague as to prejudice the appellant. The order of the High Court was therefore set aside and the appellant was directed to be detained forthwith.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. The charges were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer assisted in her going away from her parents house. "Rao" acquiesced in the girl being met by the sepoy of the unit and "Rao 's daughter elope with a sepoys". He was removed from service on April 9, 1959. The Central Government directed removal from service of Capt. section K. Rao under r 14 of Army Rules, 1954. By memorandum dated September 4,1958 Rao was called upon to submit his explanation by way of defence regarding the allegations against him. The respondent submitted his explanation and the Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory. On April 9 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service. Rao filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from serv ice on the ground that r.14 of the Rules, 1955, inter alia, provided that "the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the service any person subject to this Act". The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r 14 was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that r, 14 of Rules 1954, which provided for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45, was ultra rites and that r .14 of Army Act, 1954, was not ultra vires. HELD: The High court was right in holding that rr. 14 and 15 were framed in exer cise of the powers conferred by section 191 of the , r. 1 of the Indian Rules, and subject to section 19 of the Act. Rule 14 is such a rule : it is therefore, not ultra rites.

The appellant was a Panchayat. The Panchayat Samiti of Kanhan Pipri, which was constituted under the C.P. and Berar Panchayat Act, 1946, framed bye laws called the Maharashtra Village Panchayats and Fees Rules, 1960. Under r. 3(b) of the said rules, octroi duty shall be imposed on goods coming within its local limits as per Schedule I to item 2 of Sch. 1 annexed to this Part. The appellant challenged the validity of the levy of octroi by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the octroi duty was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law and therefore, quashed the resolution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The fixing of the octroi limit with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy. Under Rule 3(d), what the panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make the choice as regards two things i.e., the tax or fee imposed and the rate at which it is levied. The inhabitants of the village would be entitled to object only to these two matters, namely, (1) the tax, fee or fee to be levied; and (2) the rate. which it imposes and the rates at which the tax is levied, and the manner in which it was levied. [222 B C] (ii) The High Courts have placed a wrong interpretation on r. 5 of the Rules. Under the circumstances there would be no difficulty in dealing with questions of fact.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold, manufactures shroffs and dealers in gold. The Gold Control Act, 1968 was passed for the purpose of regulating money lending business in gold and ornaments. Section 28 of the Act provides that the Administrator shall have regard to the policy and purposes of the Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. The appellant challenged the validity of section 28 on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been expressly indicated in sec. 28 by reference to which the Administrator is required to exercise his power. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 5(1) of the , provides that where the Administrator has regard to policy and purpose of the provisions of the Central Act afford more than sufficient guidance for the Administrator to give a hearing dealer who seeks permission under this section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission, the grant or renewal of a license to a dealer. [954F] 2. The object of enacting and the Scheme affords sufficient guidelines to the administrator in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. 5(i) of Act. In fact, section 28 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. [951B C] 3. The main object in putting the Act on the Act is to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and use and Possession of, gold ornaments and articles of gold and articles thereof connected therewith or incidental thereto. [940C] 4. The various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in Gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. It is also clear that the restrictions which have been imposed in secs. 28 are meant to prevent the circumvention of other provisions of Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention thereof should not be premitted. Having regard to this position which obtains in the case section 28 cannot be struck down on the grounds of excessive delegated delegation of power. [942D E] 5. Section 29 confers an unguided and uncanized power without anything criteria for deciding the discretion vested in him under section 28. The scheme affords adequate guidance to Administrator in matters of exercise of his power, and it is clear that no express rule prescribing the conditions or circumstances under which the permission can be granted or refused (1) 955 has been framed nor any particular guide line has been expressly mentioned in sec tion 28 by referring to whichthe Administrator is obliged to exercise its power.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of the lower appellate court that the transfer was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (No. XIX of 1951). In appeal to this Court it was contended that the properties were alienated from time to time and as a result of the last alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. HELD : The High Court was in error in reversing the decision of the courts below by holding that the title of the temple had not been lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. [123 B] The fact that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of a temple, but in their individual character as owners of the said properties, did not show that they were holding the same as managers of the trust. There was evidence to show that the respondents had been removed from management of the temples and other persons have taken up the position as de facto managers. The High court was in wrong in reversing this decision of courts below. [124 C D] Gnanasbanda vs Sri Pachaikanta Udayavar Temple, Mad. 127 and Damodar Das 's case, , referred to. In the present case, the alienor had been appointed by the trustees of a Hindu endowment on the basis that it belonged to the religious endowments. The respondents were appointed as trustees of the properties by respondent No. 3 who was acting as de jure managers of respondent No,. 4. There is evidence to showed that the parties purported to have transferred all their properties and left the village.

The appellant, who had retired from the firm and was running a cinema theatre, applied to the District Magistrate under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the proposed site, a detailed description of which was furnished in the plan annexed to the application. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979. On appeal, the District Judge held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who was declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the APSara Theatre and directed that the requisite licence for running the Cinema Theatre may be issued to him under the Act and Rules. On July 22, 1969, a notice to the appellant, proposing to commence an venture to construct and operate an air conditioned cinema in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu, in Collaboration with two osher persons, namely Todar Mal and Kishan Kumar in their own names shall not be their personal property but shall be their Personal property. The notice was served upon the appellant on July 22. 1969, by a letter dated September 24, 1980, requesting that the required licence for starting the Cinema theatre may be granted "in the name" of the "premises of Apsar Theatre situated at Gandhi Nagar Jammu". On June 17, 1969 the Superintendent of Police, Jammu City, reported to the Deputy Commissioner that the construction of the theatre and installation of the cinema building and equipment had all been completed pursuant to the permission granted by the Government. The Deputy Commissioner rejected the request of TodarMal and Krishan Kumar on the ground that the G renewal could not he made in his name any other than original licensee. On June 18, 1969 a notice was issued to the respondent under section 6 of the Act calling upon him to submit an application for a declaration that the licence granted by him was the sole license of the appellant. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court and the same was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice inasmuch as the said procedure had not been followed by the District Collector, Jammu; (ii) that even though the licence had originally been issued in the names of Ved Gupta and six of the partners automatically acquired an interest in the licence, the other partners automatically acquire interest in it; (iii) that under the provisions of the statute prohibiting exhibition of cinematograph films in public by any one other than licensee or his authorised representative, the licensing authority was vested with exclusive jurisdiction to suspend a licence pending the proceed ings for such revocation and (iv) that since Ved Gupta had been expelled from the partnership and had thereby ceased to be connected with the firm, he did not have the possession of the premises and he was not entitled to claim a renewal of his licence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned order is one obviously passed by the district Magistrate in exercise of his function of administering the provisions and the Rules clearly include the power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the Statute. [595D] 1.2 In the instant case, the impugned orders are one purely passed by a District Magistrate in the exercise of its functions of administering cinematograph films and the powers to administer and enforce the provisions thereof and the implied power to control the exhibition of the cinematograph films is publicly exhibited by persons other than licensees.

The appellants were displaced persons. The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellants, Exhibit A, which was a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. There was a sale of the stock of raw materials unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars and other movables which were in the mills and the factory with elaborate provisions for the determination and payment of price therefor in 979 due course. The appellants were unable to remove the stocks or raise any money on the security thereof and to send daily reports to the Custodian of the transactions with reference thereto. The Custodian issued a notice to the appellants under section 12 of the Act, calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not he evicted. The notice was served on the appellants on the ground that they had no authity or jurisdiction to issue the notice in question under section 13 of the , and that the Custodian had power to cancel the lease granted by him, and that no directions could be given under section 10 of the . The appellants contended that the action taken by the Custodian under section 8 was illegal. Held, that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice and that it was not open to the appellant to contend that it conferred no authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. The operative portion of the section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and does not include any contract between the parties. The provisions of section 12 do not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. It cannot be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative portion.

The appellant was a minor son of Raghubir Singh. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th May 1976 held that Surendrapal Singh and his son Surendrapal singh were entitled to retain Bighas and 8 Biswas as held by the lower courts. The sub Divisional Officer then came to the conclusion that Surendra Pal Singh was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March 1963 and was only 13 years when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional officer on 5th of May 1976. He, however, held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub Divi sion Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1955 and not according to the new Law i. e. Act of 1954. The Board then went on to hold that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and Surendrapal Kaur formed one unit and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas & 8 Biswas. It was thus held that although the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The High Court also did not go into the merits of the controversy nor it thought it advisable to into it and it would be for the Sub Division Officer, to decide it in the light of the observations of the Board. It is clear from the language of Section 221 of the Act that the Board of Revenue has general powers of superintendence and supervision over all Revenue Courts. It can neither ignore any specific provision of law nor does it convert its powers of supervision into judicial powers. [724G H; 725A B] Kana and others vs Board of revenue Rajasthan, ; , followed.
