The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Dy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the recommendation of Justice palekar was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. Aggrieved by the decision of the High court the appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The law reports published by the Ist Respondent contain information about recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these matters in which the public is interested. [785B] 2. The Law reports published from Delhi which publishes the judgments rendered by the Supreme court within a day or two cannot be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. They believe that faster the decisions are published in their law reports which are published periodically either weekly, fortnightly or monthly. They believed that f Master the decisions were published in its law reports and newspapers reports which were being published regularly either weekly or fortnightly. They belief that fsters the decisions is published in the law books of the public are interested in knowing the contents and the effect of the decisions. [783C D] 3. The expression 'newspaper ' is usually applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers and periodicals have been included in addition to many others which deal exclusively with party affairs. [784E F] 4. The word 'new 'spaper" is generally applied ( except so far the concerns the relevant class of Trade newspapers and periodics have not been excluded from the list of newspapers. In fact, the law Reports published by them may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. The provisions of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898, the Indian Posts Offices Act 1898, and the Delivery of Books and Newspapers Act, 1956, are almost as important statutes, rules and regulations passed by the competent legislatures and other bodies since they affect public generally. It is well known that the decisions of the superior courts while they settle the disputes between the parties to the proceedings in which they are given they are the sources of law so in far as all others are concerned. As soon as a decision is rendered the members of the Public would be interested in knew it and the consequence of the decision. [781F G] 5. The Indian Post offices Act, 1939, and its corresponding laws published by Central Government on the publication of the said law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by them.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February 1965. On or about 9th February, 1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it was alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. This agreement was in writing and this was for a period of five years i.e., from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970. The appellant continued by virtue of that agreement. It was alleged in the plaint that this was executed on 9th Febru ary, 1965 and it is alleged that the appellant continued to charge less rent or triable profits. The trial Judge decreed the suit filed by the respondent and ordered eviction of the appellant from the premises. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by him under Article 227 of the Constitution. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent was not a licensee; (ii) the agreement was for leave and licence and the appellant was not claiming protection as a sub tenant under the Rent Act but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. ' no preliminary issue was to be framed; (iii) the High Court had wrongly interfered with the finding of the trial court that the respondent had failed to prove that he was a subtenant; and (iv) the appellant had not proved that he had given the workshop to respondent for conducting business. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The agreement in question is a licence and not a lease. [1063C] 2.2 In determining whether an agreement creates between the landlord and tenant merely of that licensor and licensee of that status or of licensor, the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. [1166D] 2(a) There is no simple litmus test to distinguish a lease as defined in section 105, from licence as defined under section 52 of the Easements Act, but the character of the transaction turns on the operative intent of the party. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & others vs Shri Vishwa Nath & Ors., [1987] 2 Scale 27, referred to. 1(b) The test of exclusive possession is important and the decisive factor is the knowledge of licensor and licensor of that licensee and merely of the licensor and of that licence of licensor.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before merger of former Dhol Purshedpur State into the Matsya Union. The United State of Rajasthan became the Part B State of Dholpur in which the former State of Darbhanga had merged on March 17, 1948. Thereafter the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. The respondent was not able to export the entire quantity of 15000 maund for which the permit was granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export the whole quantity of 45,000 miles for which he had paid export duty. He could only export the full quantity of 180,427 maunds and 20 seers of churi before December 2. 1947. The State Government refused to refund the advance duty but the respondent filed a suit against the State of Ajmer and contended that in view of article 295(2) of the Constitution the State was bound by the obligation of the latter State of jindpur to refund any amount due to the respondents. Held, that when the new State continued all the old laws till they were repealed, amended or altered by the new state, the old law would continue until they were superseded and the new States could not be regarded as an existing State. The rights arising under the old statutes were governed by the Covenant which took over the assets and liabilities of the new sovereign and was not bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the erstwhile State of Junagarh. The new sovereign had no authority to make laws in respect of the rights flowing from the old ones or to alter them. The old laws were always continued till they came into existence after their respective covenants, and it was not necessary that the new ruler should continue to exist until they became the new Government.

The appellants were carrying on business in cotton and groundnut. The Market Committees of the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. On May 18, 1951, the State Government issued G. 0. No. 251 (Food & Agriculture Department) extending the provisions of the Act to Ramanathapuram and Tirunelveli District in respect of cotton and groundnuts. The appellants challenged the validity of the provisions on the grounds that the provisions Of the Act were not unreasonable restrictions upon their fundamental right to do business, that they did not violate any of the objects for which they were enacted but defeat their purpose; that the Act was a colourable legislation aimed at controlling the buying and selling of agricultural crops by providing suitable and regulated markets and regulated by eliminating middlemen and bringing forward market for sale of such commercial crops. The Act was passed on July 25, 1933, and the Rules framed thereunder were duly constituted. On January 9, 1953, the Government directed constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar and markets at (1) Virudhuagar; (2) Rajapalayan and (3) Sattur in Ramanathapuram District. The market committees were duly formed and on January 9. 1953, they issued notice stating that all the traders in cotton groundnut and groundnut who failed to take out licences on or before February 15, 1953 were liable to prosecution. The respondents challenged the constitutional validity of these provisions on two grounds: (1 ) that the sections of the Madras Commercial Crops Act (Mad XX of 1933) which provided for the better regulation of buying and sale of commercial crops in the State were not reasonable restrictions on their right to carry on trade; (ii) that the impugned provisions violated article 19(1)(f) or (g) of the Constitution as they did neither achieve the object for which it was enacted, nor contravened their purpose. HELD: (i) The Act is an integrated one and regulates the buying, selling and selling commercial crops by making suitable arrangements for marketing the goods; (b) that a person who has a licence to trade in and about the place where the market is fixed, is deprived of his livelihood, which is an unreasonable restriction upon his right to deal with business unless it is clearly established that the provision are too drastic, unnecessarily harsh and overreach the scope of the object to achieve which it is enacted. It is therefore necessary to scrutinize the provisions and the rules made thereunder to ascertain whether the restrictions imposed are not reasonable. [103 E F] (ii). The Act has been passed on June 25, 1932, and it regulates the purchase and selling agricultural crops in a particular area and calls for objections and suggestions to be made within a prescribed time. After the market was established, it is established that it is expedient to provide for the proper regulation of the buying or selling of commercial crop in the locality where admittedly the entire scheme of building a net work of markets could not be finished within a predictable time, is not a reasonable restriction on their rights to do so. [104 E F]. (iii) The object of the impugned Act was to protect the growers, the traders and the buyers from unnecessary expenditure which they could not afford. The provisions of section 5 are too harsh and severe overreaches the scope for exploitation in dealings.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced it to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference of opinion between the High Court and the Supreme Court on the question of guilt. [1097 D] (ii) The fact that Pandu rang, though armed with an axe, though under a stick or sticks, he did no more than inflict a comparatively light head injury is not sufficient to bring home the conclusion that Pandi rang was the complainant because he did not want to enter a woman 's name and so picked up her from the nearest male relative. He says that she saw Narsabai and others present to tell them what had happened, but that they went away when the eye witnesses arrived after it bad thought of a suitable tale and found likely victims for their plot. [ 1097 E] (iii) The High court was wrong in holding that section 378 of the Code did not abrogate or modify that provision. It is well established that a common intention presupposes prior concert. Several persons can simultaneously attack a man and each can have the same intention, namely the intention to kill, and each could inflict a separate fatal blow and yet none would have the common intention required by the section because there was no prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan. In a case like that each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the act.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Assistant Engineer in class II service with effect from 25.5.1954 and was later promoted as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service on 4.9.1965. He was later reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer, Class I in service but on 4th September 1965 he was reverted to his substantive post of Asstt. Engineer in the pay scale of Rs. 25.6. 1954. The petitioner challenged that order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the impugned order of compulsory retirement made against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) as the petitioner had not attained the age of 55 years by the date of the order, he had crossed the age o f 55 years; (ii) in any other case after he has attained the maximum age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and therefore on the date when the impugned orders were served on him, Fundamental Rule 56(j)(i) was not contravened when the order was made; (iii) the petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class 11 service but only on 4 9 1965 when he was compulsorily retired under Fundamental Rule 57(j). Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The contention of the respondent that the similarly placed persons had gone before the Delhi High Court challenging the orders of compulsory retire ment and the Delhi high Court relying upon Tahiliani 's case cannot be accepted. [638D] 2.1 Rule 56 (j)(ii) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a capacity, and not on an officiating basis only. The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to the substantive post is not at all relevant in the matter of exercising powers of compulsory retiring. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his original post before the power of compul sation retirement is exercised, the Government serv ice must be taken to be in Class II or Class II service or post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). [639E F] 2(a) The possibility that such incumbent be sent back lo his substantive posts is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56. The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to classify Gov ernment servants into two categories and sub cl.(i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the rele vant time are in Class 1 or Class 11 Service or post even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis. Instances are where officers are promoted to Class I or Class III service or posts even when they hold a post in either classally or temporarily, on officiating capacity and such officiation lasts for a number of years. Officiating promotion certainly does not confer a right to the Post and at any time the Government servants may be sent to his pre existing post. [643B C] 2.(b) The purpose behind it is to classified Gov erment servants in Class III or Class I Service or posts as covered by sub clause(i).

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. The appellant Corporation contested the claim on the ground that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there had been concluded contract of insurance between the respondents and the appellant Corporation and, therefore, it was not a concluded contract. The High Court held that there were no concluded contracts between the respondent and the Life Insurance Corporation of India. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. [353B] (2) The expression "underwriting and revivals" signifies liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. The word "underwrite" is used in Marine insurance but the expression used in the Marine Insurance Act, but the expressions used in it are of general import. When an insurance policy becomes effective well settled by the authorities, it may be stated that it is the Divisional Manager who was competent underwrite policy for Rs 50, 000 and above. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is acceptance not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [355C D] MacGillivray & Parkington Insurance Law, Seventh Edition p. 1267 at page 222 referred to. (3) The word 'underwriting ' signifies liability ' under section 2(6). It is true that normally the expression "inwrite ' is used but the phrase used in marine insurance but in the expression 'underwrites ' is employed in Marine Insurance, but in our opinion, the dictionary meaning of the expression is used to denote liability under. The definition also indicates what is intended to convey acceptance. Mere delay in giving an offer does not mean acceptance. A mere delay in making an offer cannot be construed as acceptance, prima facie, acceptance must be communicated to the offer. [356E F] Macgillray &Parkington on Insurance Law Sixth Edition p 1267 referred to and relied on. (4) The mere execution of the insurance policy is not an acceptance. It is a acceptance. There is no evidence that the Assistant Divisional Manager had accepted the proposal on the contrary. He had stated otherwise.

The plaintiffs applied for a certificate under articles 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The High Court granted an interim injunction restraining the Bank from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s V.S. Tractors Export, Moscow, Moscaow, Nos. 4012/68. The plaintiffs applied to the High Court for revocation of the certificate granted by the Madras High Court on the ground that the order of the Judicial Commissioner of Sind vacated an ex parte injunction granted by him. The appellants contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to stay the proceedings and remanded the case to him. Held, that the application for revocation was not maintainable as the decision on the question did not finally dispose of the dispute between the parties. The order refusing to grant an interim order did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. The proceeding instituted on the complaint was not part of or incidental to the proceedings for determination in the civil court; it was thereafter for the trial court trying the complaint to decide whether the offence complained of was committed by the appellant. The proceedings for filing a complaint under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were a self contained proceeding and was finally disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complain under section 205 read with section 114, I.P.C. The application for the revocation of certificate granted to M/S V. Trails Export, had not been decided and it was not open to the appellants to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of grey cloth in the hands of the processor and who had made them to be sold by the processor, challenged the assessment on the ground that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey fabrics in the market at which they would be selling the processed goods. The Tribunal rejected the claim holding that the market value of a processed fabric was the value at which he would be purchasing the processed cloth and excise duty would include only the price or deemed price at which the processed fabrics would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. The assessable value is the value which the processing machine would leave. The factory gate here means the "deemed factory" as if the processed product was sold by that process. In order to explain the position it is made clear that the declared value of processed fabric will be the price at Which he would sell the processed commodity and excise duties would include the only price or the deemed price, at which it would be sold the processing goods in the Market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable valuation of the processing cloth and duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price would at which goods would be sell the processing materials would give a declaration to the processed as to what would be its price at the factory gate for the processed job work. [346B C] 1.2. The market value at the time of sale is Rs.30, being the value thereof plus the value Of the grey cloth plus the cost of the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be, the correct as sessable value. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processing for processing on job work basis, would give declaration to that processor as to how would he sell the grey fabrics and excise Duty would be chargeable to the manufacturer on that date provided that declaration as the price of the grey fabric plus the manufacturing profit and/or manufacturing expenses would be paid to the processors on that foundation. The value of such grey cloth or fabric plus cost of job work would be Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be RS.30 being the valuation of grey fabric or fabric with the job worked plus manfac ture and expenses [346C D] 1:3. The price at what the processed textile fabric would leave is the processor factory plus its profit. Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another person are purchased by the same information is required relating to the prices at which such manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person authorised to discharge all the liabilities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The 'deemed factory ' means the 'deemed Factory ' as if it is the processed Fabric of the fabric or with the manufacturing profits and the job done plus the manufacture profit and the manufacturing expenses, but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor `s expenses, costs and charges and profit plus the processing work done. [347D E] 1 :4. The expression 'deemed ' factory ' in Rule 174(1) of the Rules enjoins that where goods ownedby one person arc manufactured by the other information is needed relating to price atwhich the said manufacturer is sold the said commodity would include, only the prices or deemed value at Which the processed material would leave, which will either be included in the price At the factory ' gate for processing fabric. The manufacturer who entrusting cotton or yarn made fabric of manufic turing profits and expenses to the rejected processed fabrics and the excise duty payable would include any price or other subsequent profits or expenses but not an amount equal to the value as may be determined by the Central Government in accordance with Rule 174.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by the respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the Single Judge. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the amending Act, the Panchayat Samities had lost its power to appoint him as a Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service and since the appellant was not appointed as such, he could not have been absorbed in Government Service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, which has been recognised by the State Legislature on June 13, 1973. [775B] 2. The contention that by virtue of section 13(4), the Panchayat samities had become divested of its power under the Amending Acts of 1973, the appellant could not improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13. 1973 when the Amending came into force is unsustainable. [771C] 3. The fact that the appellant had been promoted as a head clerk prior to June 13 1973 does not improve the position for this simple reason. [753D E] 4. The rights to be consider for promotion, whether the Panchayat takes the right to appoint the appellant to the post in which he was employed by the Samiti until he was absorbed in government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed, are not affected by section 33(3) of Act. [764E F] 5. The State Government had no power to place at the disposal of a Panchayat Samiti any of its servants as are required for the implementation of schemes connected therewith and for such other duties and functions as may he assigned to them by the panchayat Samiti until they were absorbed in the Government service or retired in such a manner as might be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section14(4). the Panchayat had lost their power of making appointments to it.

The appellants filed a suit for declaration and possession of the property in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding that the Amauli properties were owned by Math and the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar installed in the Math, which included the properties in village Amauli. On appeal, the High Court allowed both the appeals and held that the Mahant was entitled to the benefit of the trust property as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum and must therefore be regarded as property belonging to the Math or the deity; and that the suit was not maintainable in view of section 53 of the U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the properties which constitute the personal property of Uma Shankar Yati were not liable to be regarded by the Math as property belong to the deity or the idol. [663C] 2.1 The mere fact that a Mohunt is ancetic does not raise any presumption that a property in his possession is not his personal property. Strictly speaking there is no presumption either one way or the other, and in each case the burden is upon the plaintiff to establish that the property In respect of which he is asking for possession are properties to the possession of which the Mahant is askingfor possession. [665E] 2:2. The mere circumstance that a co Mohunt was generally his personal properties cannot be regarded to be evidence as belonging to or the temple. As has been observed, there can be no presumption whether the property can be said to belong to or deity or is the personal properties of the Math. [662F G] 3:3. The onus resting on the party who makes the claim rests on the person who makes it. The burden of proof resting on him who makes a claim depends on the plaintiff. In each case, the burden of proving resting on his party who made the claim lies. [664H] 4:4. The evidence disclosed that Mahant Shivshankar Yati was held in high regard on account of his personal learning and attainments, and had a large number of chelas including many affluent persons from whom he received personal bhents or pranamis of large amounts of money. His personal property, on his death included cash, sovereigns and properties which included some affluent persons who had passed through the grihastha ashram. Some of them continued to possess and even to acquire personal property after taking sanyas. It was also found that Mahant Shri Shivs Shankar Yathi was held by high regard in respect of both properties. The revenue records mentioned the name of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yathi, who executed a waqf deed on November 12, 1892 bequeathing various properties to him and his personal funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivsker Yati. On his death he was succeeded by Mahant Shiv Shankar Yatha. He had also inherited the personal estate of Shri Shivbaran Yati and did not belong to Math or deity. The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for consolidation of their lands with those of the appellants in the year 1949 and instead allotted to them land in substitution of their names in the village Karodian. The Assistant Custodian, however, rejected the application on the ground that the appellants had a wrongly fitted in the villages Karodian and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order cancelling their allotments on the grounds (1) that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of allotment in favour of the appellant and that the cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952 was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land and (2) that the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955 was invalid because it was not based upon any of the grounds set out in the 6th condition. Held:(1) The provisions of section 19(1)(f) of Evacuee Property Act are not inconsistent with any other law for the time being in force and they must prevail over the general provision. (2)(a) The words "any property" in section 19 of the 1954 Act are to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other Law for the lime being in operation, but subject to the rules that may be made under the Act the managing officer or managing corporation constituted under the , would be in conflict with those conferred by section 19 Of the 1954 act on a managing officer appointed or managing corporations only and no one else. (b) The appellants ceased to hold and had lost possession of the Raikot lands before the publication of the notification and were thus not entitled, to the protection of the section.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District expunged/Associate Regionalmasters of Girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (emale 's Branch). The advertisement inviting applica tion from eligible candidate was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and written. The viva voce test was over, on the basis of the results thereof. The ap pointment for the first time was to be called for interview but was also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry being over, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that there was improper feeding into the calculation limit. The Public Service commission decided to cancelled the entire ap point ment examination and called for a final interview. On account of improper feeding in the written examination, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tion. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the viva voce examination, it was factually estab lished that the Public service Commission decided to cancelling the entire recruit ment examination. [125B] 1.2.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass as his Chela he was entitled to manage the properties of the Dera and that the appellant had no right to recover possession of the property. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. [489C] In the instant case, the suit was for possession and management of the dera and its properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be the de facto mahant against Som Dass as de facto mator. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Das was elected to be mahant did not affect the question whether the right in the subject matter of the suit devolved upon him. [490E] In Roshan Lal Kapur vs Chand Kapur, ; , relied on. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matters of the litigation and the interest is the interest of the person who was the party to the suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest during the pendency of a suit, the appeal may be continue against the persons acquiring the interests with the permission of the court. When the suit is instituted by or between a person who dies or retire during the course of a proceeding but that Suit may be continuing against the other person acquiring it with the right to sue the person entitled to such attachment to the benefit of sub rule (1). [490B C] In this case, when a suit was brought by a person against or against another in a party capacity and the appellant was not bound to take on record his legal representatives, then the appellant could be added as parties under Order 22, Rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [491C D] In such a case the successor to the head of the mutt or manager of the temple may be substituted as a party under this rule. The words 'interest" in the rule means "interest in the properties i. e., the Subject matter of suit and the interests is the property of the persons who was party to it". When a case is brought against oragainst a person acquiring interest with leave of court, he also applies if the head or manager or the mutttt or Manager of the Temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such case the predecessor in office.

The first respondent, a political party called Telugu Desam was swept to power to retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the age of 55 years. The Chief Minister justified the reduction of the retirement age from 58 to 60 years on the ground that it had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths. Over 18,000 Government employees and 10,000 public sector employees were retired as a result of the order. The first respondent challenged the Ordinance on the grounds that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution for reducing the age to 55 years on account of the increase in the age Of retirement from 58 and 55 years to 60 by the Government of Andhra Pradesh by a notification dated October 29, 1979 and nothing happened since then to justify reduction of his age to 58. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of the Ordinance were arbitrary and irrational and violative of articles 14 and16 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the impugned Act was bad because it was passed in a hurry, as a consequence of which the Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the age; (ii) the Government was estopped from reducing the retirement value to 55 and since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age, it did not justify reduction in the retirement of the employees beyond 60 years; (iii) the State exchequer would have to find and pay Rs. 70 crores on one single day by way of retirement benefits, for which no budgetary provision was made; (iv) the proviso to rule 2 was deleted from the Fundamental Rules, because it is arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it seeks to achieve; (v) the amendment to the Fundamental Rule was not violative of article 311(2); (vi) the second proviso to Rule 2 was also invalid as it was not based on any recommendation of the Commission. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned Act is bad because the Government has reviewed the situation arising out of enhancement of the superannuation age from 55 to 58 and that, the present measure was intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees and since it is an important factor in the attractiveness of Government service, fixation of retirement age at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [602C D] 2.

The assessee purchased certain raw materials in the State without paying tax thereon, in view of the provisions contained in section 24(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee sold these goods out of India and exported those goods out Of India. On these facts it was claimed that the assessee is not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1). This claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the only facts in sary (or) are identical; (ii) the assessee was not liable for payment of purchase tax because the sales effected by the assessees fall within one of the three exempted categories set out in section 9 (1)(b); and (iii) the transaction is covered by section 5(3). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessee are not charge able to tax either u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). [365B] 2.1 The provisoes to section 27(a)(iv), in particular, make a clear contrast between sales falling under sub section (3) and those failing under sub s.(1) and the provisoes inserted with retrospective effect from 27th May 1971 a point of time when actually a prede cessor Act is enacted. [365C] 2:2 The proviso to section 4(a) of Haryana Sales tax Act, 1976 makes a clear distinction between sales failing under subsection (3), and those falling under section 5 (1) but not under section 6. [366D] 3.2 In the instant case, the assessee purchased raw materials inside the State of Haryana but paid no tax thereon. The raw materials were purchased by the asses seeers from outside the State in accordance with the provisions of section 24 of the Act. The sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act are not laible to tax under section 4. [367E] 3:3.1 In the present case, there can be no levy of purchase Tax under section 7(1), because the sale effected by assessees fall outside one of these three exempted category set out therein in section9(1)(a) and (b). The raw material purchased by them are not charged to tax u/r 9(2).

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The sales tax authorities assessed the appellant to purchase tax on its turnover including those sales. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase sales tax. The appellant 's appeals were dismissed by the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales were effected on forward contracts and not on shipped basis, that the goods remained their property till the goods had been brought on board the ship and so the sales could be exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. HELD : The High Court was right in its conclusion that the appellant ' goods remained the sellers ' property till they had passed beyond the territorial waters of India. [928 C] The fact that the bill of lading was retained by the seller, did not make it a case of "delivery ". The words " delivered ", when the goods cross the customs barrier, were used to indicate an intention of the parties that the property in the goods would pass till after payment. The question whether there was such a different agreement had to be decided on a consideration of all the surrounding circumstances. [936 D] The ordinary rule inContract contracts is that it is the duty of the buyer to obtain the necessary export licence. If at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate purchasing the dealer has the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person who is not a registered dealer, it cannot strictly be said that the declaration has not been carried out. The scheme of the Legislature clearly shows nothing more than that the title in the property shall pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the ordinary limits of India or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. Whichever view is taken there is nothing to indicate that the intention to comply with the requirements of el. 5(2) of ' the Exports (Control) Order, 1954, was to be given effect to. [970 G H] The words ' delivered " in cl. 5 (2) are wide enough to include a registered dealers or anybody else. It is not correct to say that it does not commence till the ship has passed beyond its territorial waters. The intention of parties that in compliance with the requirement of el, 5(1) of Export Control Order, 1955, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the point of time when they crossed this frontier.

Nor can s127(3), (b), subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor cannot, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of payment 'under any customary or Personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the statutory project can secure validation if the court is to pay true homage to the Constitution. [80C] 2(i) Section 127(2)(b), does not contemplate divorcees who have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section125, but fairly then section 127.(3) requires as a sine qua non for its application, neglect by neglect or father. The obligation cannot be whittled down by any ritual exercise rooted in custom. No construction which leads to frustration of the constitutional scheme is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic purpose but pedantic purposeful. [81D E] 2.(ii) Section 125 of Criminal Procedure code requires as sine qua Non for its applica tion, neglect or husband by neglect by husband and father. [82E F] 3(i). The words printed in the particular Code are "the" meaning of meanings is derived from values in a given society and its legal system. Article 15(3 ) has compelling, compassionate relevance in the context of section 125 and the benefit Of doubt. If any in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill wife used and the derelict divorcee. This social perspective granted, the resolution of all disputes projected is easy. Surely Parliament, in keeping with article 15(1) and deliberate by design made a special provision to help women in distress cast away by divorce. Protection against moral material and abandonment material and legitimate abandonment of claim which does not have the Special statutory right. [83G H; 83A] 4.2 The intention of the legislature is that Parliament intended divorcees should not derive double benefit. If the first payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 128(3C) (a), it will be unjust to obliterate that claim. Nor can section 127 operate to nullify that claim, nor can s128 be invoked to negate that claim.[81D] 5. The fact that in the normal course an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the Magistrate at the trial level, is no ground of non neglect.

The appellant was a bidder for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27.3.88 and he gave the shop of Beni country liquor to him. The name of the appellant did not deposit dak amount. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Collector, which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order directing that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect o future contracts under the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation of the bid of the ap pellant is concerned, that is not affected. This order will not prevent the State Government or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for ragging the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law i.e. giving the appellant due notice and an opportunity of making representation. [869C D] 1.2 The last portion, of the Order directing that appellant be placing in the Black list in regard of future contract under the orders passed by the Collector was set aside, and so far as it directs black listing the appellant in respect thereof, the order directed that the appella nt shall not prevent State Government from taking immediate steps forcasting the appellant.

The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 for fixation of fair rent. The Rent Controller held that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the lease deed and that they had not constructed any of the premises thereon. The High Court in revision held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation Of fair rent in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that: (1) the Rent Control Tribunal had no juris diction to fix the fair rent; (2) the respondents had not been given notice to quit under section 111(h) of the Act and, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent controller 's order in respect of the Premises covered by exhibit P1 was only an amount of rent; and (3) what the fair Rent Controller has to do is to satisfy himself that the person seeking eviction or fixation of rent is a "landlord" who has prima facie, the right to receive the rents of the property in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Rent Court is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent Proce dure by the terms of the statute itself. [557C] 2.1 In a proceeding under the Act whether it be for fixation o fair rent or eviction, the tenant may raise several objections. But, this Court cannot go into the question of title to immovable property and that a civil court cannot be barred from examining a claim merely because the question may have had to be considered by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. [511E] 2(a) The jurisdiction is a vested in tho Rent Controller by the term of the section itself. It is not open to one of the parties to contend that the decision given by the Court of Small Causes, which has become final between the parties, is a total nullity which can be completely ignored. [657F] (b) The question on which the jurisdiction of civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the fair price of the suit premises. If the civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there was relationship of landlord and tenant and a tenant, the Controller has no jurisdic tion to entertain an application except by a landlord or a tenant. [577G] (c) The expression "landlord ' is not defined in section 2(g) of Act. It means any person who has, prima facie and reasonably, the rights to receive rents of property in dispute. In order to decide whether the denial of the landlord 's title by the tenant is bona fide, it would be open to the owner to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil Court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil suit.

The Mysore State Civil Service ( Integra tion) Rules 1960 provided for filing objections only against the preliminary provisional Inter State Seniority List and do not provide any provision for filing objection or appeal against the final inter State Seniority list as per Annexure 'B '. The petitioner, whose date of birth is given as 28th June 1915, has retired from service on 31st March, 1954. He was given a due opportunity to object to the provi sional list. The High Court held that the combined gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Mysore State Service Integra tory Rules 1960 provide for filing an objection only against tho preliminary provisional inter state Seniority list although he was given due opportunity; and (ii) the rules had not been complied with in as much as the Central Government has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act. HELD: The combined gradation lists dated April, 6,1962 so faras category 6 are concerned, are ultra vires. [830 B] Union of India vs G.M. Shankariah & Ors., ; , followed. In P.K. Roy 's case this Court had held upon a concession by the Attorney General that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the , must be given an opportunity to objecting to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. [826 C D] The State Government is bound to ensure a fair and equitable treatment to officers in the matter of integration of services.

The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March 1979 was amended by para 174 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said policy. One of the aforesaid facilities was grant of an Additional licence in terms of Para 176 of the Policy. One such grant was granted on or after April 1, 1988 subject to the conditions laid down in this regard in the Import Export Policy 1991 88. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant Of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licences. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "other Products" during the year 1977 78. The Petitioners filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution before the High Court and the said writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court. Hence these two special leave petitions. On behalf of the petitioners it has been contended that sub para (10) of Para 218 which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export House Houses prior to April 1 1988 will cease to be valid for import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and Part A of this Policy, subject to conditions laid therein, subject also to the condition laid down therein in this respect. The respondents submitted that all Export houses who have been granted Additional licences prior to 1.4.1988 will cease lo be valid only for import items of items which were banned for import by the holder of an additional licence. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to import all other items whether canalised or otherwise in accordance With the relevant rules. These licences will also cease to he valid for the import of item of raw material, components, consumables and spares appearing in Appendix 6, List 8, Part A and Item of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by an Append Items 3 and part A) available under this Policy. [236B] 1.2 The Additional licences granted prior to the April 1. 1988 will continue to be effective for import only items of the items which are banned for imports by the holders of an addition licence. [237C D] 1:3 The petitioners who were granted Additional Licences prior to 4.1.1988 cannot avail the flexibilities in import of Item granted under Para 176. They can avail the facility that have been provided to Export houses which were granted additional licences under the Import Policy 1988 91 and it cannot be said that they have been subjected to arbitrary and hostile discrimination. [238D] 1 :4 The petitioners have failed to make out a case for interference by this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. [239E F] Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, ; , referred to. 1.5 In the Import & Exports Policy 1988 89 there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para. (4) of para 215 of the Import and Export Policy 198891. The concession made by the petitioners that they were entitled to this relaxation is different from the basis on which Additional licences were granted to the extent of 33% of the f.o.b.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at Visakhapatnam. The appellant manufactures and sells fusel oil/Srenety Monomer falling under Tariff Item 68 of the First Schedule to the Act. The goods were sold in wholesale as "naked Works and in bulk". According to the appellant, the manufacture of fusel Oil is complete and it is fully manufactured fusel oils/S stenographertyrene Monomers falling under tariff item No. 68 of First Schedule. The contention of the appellant was that the cost of packing which is of a durable nature and is returnable by the buyer to the assessee, in all other cases the cost should be included in the assessable value of the fuselon/S Sawhney Monomy Monomier. It was also contended that the price lists issued by the buyers showed the value of fuels oil/s Sawhney M Liberer at the rate which those were sold at the time of removal and delivered to the customers at the factory. The Collector held that at the relevant time the removal of the goods were delivered from the factory packed in condition and the containers were not returnable by buyer, there fore, the value had to be included as "cost of packing" in the wholesale market. On appeal, the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal held that the value could not be included under the assessable valuation of the fuel oil/MSrene M Liberers and that the drums were not delivered at the price packed in the factory by the appellant. The Tribunal further held that there was no occasion for considering the question whether the cost could be included or not, and that it should have held that "the value" could not he included in assessable value. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the cost Of packing which was of adurable nature was returnable by buyers to the asses see; (ii) the drums had been supplied by the assessee for the gas cylinders supplied by him to customers in drums and the container were not packed in terms of the price list, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector; and (iii) the packing could be excluded from the assessablevalue only when the packing was either manufactured by the assesse or is purchased by the purchaser. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The cost of such packing as is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market at the buyer 's factory gate which can be in cluded in the value for determining the "value" in relation to the excisable goods for computing the duty payable on it. [994C] 2. The price charged by the manufacturer, the cost incurred by the consumer and recovered from the buyer except where the packing is of durable character and returnable by him is not includible in the taxable value but a duable packing supplied by a buyer to his customer is made a part of the assessable Value. [952D] 3. The "cost" of such pack ing" incurred by a manufacturer when the container is supplied by it and not the manufacturer has to be necessarily included in its assessable value, but a powder or user of the packing cannot be "notionally added to, or subtracted from, the price at which the goods are sold does not include that value then it must be so included by the very force of the terms of section 4. [962E] 4. The 'cost of such Packing" referred in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act is sufficient to allow these appeals. [973G H] 5.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant produced currency notes from his possession before the file itself was kept by him in his personal custody. The prosecution case is that the appellant had taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued the practice before the notice was issued. The trial court accepted the plea of the appellant and convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that though the conviction under section 4(1) of ' the Prevention Of Corrup tion Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be awarded under section 5 and (2) of tho Prevention of Corrup tration Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [337C] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant was not even aware of the demand made by him. He had thereafter received the amount of Rs. 100 from PW 1. This conduct of the appel lant in view of the presumption arising under section4(1), if any, arising under s 4(i) of Prevention of ' Corruption Act is not attracted on the facts proved. [336E F] 2:2. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the Explanation is a true one. The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebut by ' proof and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his accumulated Leave after his retirement i.e. for a period of six months and undertaking to vacate the flat as early as possible. The company on humanitarian grounds acceded to this request and permitted the petitioner to stay on the company in the Company 's flat for six months after his death and in accordance with the company rules, he was required to pay compensation for use of the premises. After the expiry of the period, the company addressed a communication requesting the petitioner not to vacate it stating that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company Rules. Since the petitioner failed to vacate, the Company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Estate officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner. Instead of availing that opportunity, the petitioner filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution and obtained ad interim stay of the proceedings before the Estate officer. In view of this, the respondent company initiated proceedings against the petitioner for his ejectment under the Act in the Court of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court, Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat in question which had been given to him for his residence during the periods of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 630. The petitioner 's case was that the provisions contained in sub section (1) of section 630 of the Act were a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. It was further contended that the provision contained in section 630 was a penal one and therefore, must be subjected to a restrictive meaning to the term 'officer or employee ' appearing in sub s.(1) thereof. The High Court dismissed the special leave petition holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge of the Calcutta and Bombay on Amritlal Chum 's cases really fell into an error in seeking to curtail the ambit of section 631(l)(b) by giving a restrictive interpretation to the terms 'officer ' or employee" occurring in sub sec.
