The appellant, a private Devasthan or a public religious trust, was appointed as attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as "owner" of the property. The sansthan had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the values of Rs, 19,165/ and immoveable properties. The Sanad was granted by the Charity Commissioner under protest and without prejudice to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The appellant filed an application under section 18 of the Act for declaring the Sansthan to be a public charitable trust and ordered its registration as a public Trust under the Act. The Charity Commissioner after requisite notice made an enquiry into the matter in accordance with the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The Assistant Charity Commissioner held that the appellant was a private temple and not a private property and not public trust and directed its registration. The High Court set aside the order of the District Judge and held that there was no evidence of long user of the temple by the appellant except exhibit 35 and that the conclusion was highly erroneous being contrary to the one that had been reached by the District judge on appraisal of the entire documentary evidence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the appellant 's witness Ramkrishna Deshpande that they "cannot prevent people from going to the temple as the temple is meant for the Darshan by the public. The consciousness of the manager and the consciousness of devotees themselves as to the faith of the devotees themselves, as to their character depends on the particular history. [518D E] In the instant case all these tests are fulfilled. The intention of the founder that specified individuals are to have the right of worship at the shrine or the general public or any specified portion thereof is not to be deemed an independent charity in which the public or a section of it has an interest. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public temple in a given case. Even some of the tests laid down by this Court may, in a give case, be sufficient to enable the court to come to a conclusion about the character of the trust. [525G H] The High Courts were not right In giving due weight to the evidence produced by the appel lant in this case in favour of the same conclusion.

The assessee, a resident of Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 48 and 1951 49 under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The Income tax Officer issued a notice of demand on the assessee for payment of the assessed amount of tax. No payment was made. The assessee filed an application before the Assistant Collector claiming that he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said demand certified under section 46(2) of the Act. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the assessee could not be arrested and confined only to civil prison in satisfaction. The Appellate Assistant Collector held that the notice was invalid as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal, the High Court held that section 46 (2) which enabled the Collectors in different States to adopt machinery which differs from State to State, so that defaulters are treated differently in different states and that the provisions prescribing machinery were not incorporated in section 46. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Held:(i) The proviso to section 13 was enacted to be treated as crystallised and applied by the Collectors although the State laws prescribe the procedure for recovery of arrears of land revenue and there is no discrimination in the State law that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section 46, (2). The impugned law is based on a comparison of the provisions of different laws adopted by the different States for the recovery of land Revenue. The grouping of the income tax defaulters into separate categories or classes of income tax defaulter into separate category or classes which are closely akin to the purpose of the Union. The groupsing of income Tax defaulters into different categories or class of income taxes defaulters into distinct categories or categories into separate classes or categories and thus rendered them void to the extent of such inconsistency. (ii) The classification has been made State wise and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and between State and State. The classing of these income tax default into separate heads or classes cannot be regarded by vague references to the wisdom of the legislature or by indulging in pure speculation as to what might have been at the back of its mind. Per Sarkar, J. (i) Section 46(1)(2) is not violative of article 14 and is therefore void to that extent of the inconsistency between the two provisions as they originally stood and not by it subsequently amended. By this time section 13 had been amended and the warrant of arrest was issued on the 7th June 1955, that is to say, long after the amendment of the section.

The appellant company was a workmen of the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The appellant company made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' duty, 3 hours ' and 4 hours ' overtime. The workmen claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shifts with 8 hours ' work ', 2 hour ' duty ' and 2 hours " were kept variable as they depended on the tides. In 1956 the workmen who were then represented by the Port Trust General Workers ' Union made a demands for a fix recess at 8 hours and 2 hour " overtime" and the appellant company claimed that the existing system of work needed any modification. The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the new system of working needed any modifications, and that the so called period of rest was illusory since rest was inadequate since rest had been fixed, being variable it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end, depending on the exigencies of the work. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the old system of worked of the shore crew was always available on hand, and therefore, the appellant was not entitled to any fixed hours ' shift. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the system of variable recess did not satisfy the requirements of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3) of the Act and the two rules framed thereunder were applicable to some employments and only they were shown in a Schedule appended to the Act. HELD : The normal working day thus includes (a) hours of actual duty, and (b) one or more specified intervals. There is no definition of interval either in the Act or the Rules but the provisions of section 12(2) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest. If it is the latter, it is counted as actual work period. if the former, it was counted as 'actual work '. If the former is counted, it would be counted as a period of time rest provided the period is specified beforehand and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work. Having thus distinguished between periods of work and interval of time, it cannot be said that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest for rest. [640 D E] The normal day thus included (a). hours of work in a six week cannot go beyond 12 hours.

The appellant was the tenant of a house in Ghaziabad. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika with effect from October 1, 1976. The premises were let out on June 25, 1976 and the accommodation was again for the period July 25, 1977 to March 31, 1977. The suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court set aside this conclusion of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the premises were leased out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1. 1976, the provisions of the Act referred to above will not apply for 10 years from October l, 1976, and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The restriction on the right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under Section 20 and the language of Section 39 is clear that if the provisions Of this Act apply then no suit for eviction can be instituted except on the grounds specified in the sub sections of this section. [164B] Om Prakash Gupta etc. vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta etc., ; , referred to. The restriction put under Section 40 will come to the rescue of the tenant only if the suit from which revision or appeal was pending on the date of commencement of the Amendment Act i.e. 15th July, 1972 but the suit giving rise to the present appeal was filed much after the coming into force of this Act. [165C D] Om Parkash Gupta etc vs Digvijaypal Gupta & Ors., ; ; referred to and distinguished.

The appellant instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely, Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur, from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6/1 Shibtola Lane,knowingly, Calcutta. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act as he was a bika tenant under the plaintiff and the tenancy right therein. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) with the omission of section 29 Civil Courts became unable to remit ejectment suits to the controller with the result that the Act, as finally amended could not apply to pre Act suits and thika tenants could get no relief under the Act; (ii) the provisions of the Ordinance were not retrospective in operation so far as the Act was concerned; (iii) the suit was barred by section 4 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as amended up to 1953; and (iv) the appellant had failed to establish any grounds for eviction mentioned in section 3. HELD: The High Court rightly held that sections 4 and 5 were prospective and not retrospective. [184 D] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. Mahadeal Kanal Kanniodia vs administrator General of Calcutta, ; and Mahadeulol Kanal Deolal Deoral Kanaria vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; referred to.

The High Court of Allahabad, in a writ petition filed by the respondents, directed that the pay scale of Rs. 300 1,000 be revised to Rs. 150 and Rs.515 715 respectively. The State Government appointed a Pay Commission (1971 72) headed by Shri Ali Zahir. On February 1, 1973, the Pay Commission submitted its report. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers. The High Court suggested that ten posts of Bench Secretaries Grade I should be upgraded and placed in the pay scales of Rs 500 1,500 as recommended by the Pay Commis sioner. The Government accepted this recommendation and issued an order dated July 2, 1976. The respondents filed a writ peti tion challenging the said recommendations. The Writ Petition was dismissed by the High Court on November 6, 1985. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Bench Secretaries in the High Courts of Allahabad were entitled to pay scale admissible to Section Officers and not on higher scale. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not expressly declared by our Constitution to be a fundamental right. Article 39(d) of the Constitution enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws and article 16 declares that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointments to any office under the State. To them the equality clauses will have some substance if equal work is equal pay for both men and women. The equation of posts or equation of pay must be left to the Executive Government. They would be the best judge to evaluate the nature of duties and responsibilities of posts. In fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service, the Court cannot go into the question whether there could be two scales of Pay in the same cadre of persons performing the same or similar work. The differentiation made in the said cadre will not amount to discrimination. [305B C] 2. The distinction made in affidavits of interested parties is a reasonable classification. The Court cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the pay Scales have to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or mala fide either in law or in fact. [306C D] 3. The question whether a Bench Secretaries are entitled to higher pay scale and treat as a superior class to Section officers depends upon seniority cum merit or merit cum seniority. The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay. [304D E] 4. The scales of salary and allowances of Bench Secretary Grade I are determined by a Selection Committee.

The appellant Company was a Government company incorporated under the , and the entire share capital being owned by it, was wholly owned by the Government of India. The State Government contended that it was not liable to pay the entry tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. That company had been called upon by respondent 1 to pay property tax for the years 1976 77 and 1977 78 in the sum of Rs. 11 lakhs annually to the "seed capital" of the Authority in consideration of the authority agreeing not to exercise its power of taxation or levying any other charges on the assets and activities of the Company under the Act of 1973 as amended from time to time or under any other Act or notification. The appellant company disputed its liability to pay tax by virtue of the said agreement, but it was contended that since the company was owned wholly by the State Government of Madhya Pradesh and had been receiving the property tax from the State, the State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned law. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by the Act on Special Area Development Authority is limited in its scope so as not to come in conflict with the power and function of the Union to regulate and develop the mines as envisaged by the Nationalisation Act. It is true that on account of the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Parliament alone was competent to pass a law on the subject and the State legislature had no power which a Municipal Corporation or a Municipal Council has under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1956 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act,, 1961. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the state Legislature loses its competence to enact the impugned legislation, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [15D E] 2. The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on Parliament to by virtue Of Entry 54, List I read with Entry 24, List II.

The appellant was granted a lease for twenty years to the respondent for 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947 and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947 the said Balumuri Nageswara Rao agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate quarries within his estate for five years in succession commencing from January 1942 if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by the lessee during preceding year. The respondent applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah to him but nothing appeared to have happened until February 12, 1952 when a notice was issued from the office of the Board of Revenue (Andhra) calling upon the appellant to show cause within two months from the date of receipt of that notice as to why the lease should not be terminated without any compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of revenue refused to ratify the lease and terminated it under the powers delegated to it under r. 476 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate quarry quarries and from interfering with his possession and working of the slates quarries. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the termination of the respondent 's lease by the order dated December 27, 1955 was bad as it did not give three months notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act; (ii) the second Proviso to section 21(1), which provided for compensation would not be attracted and action taken by the Government under the third proviso to sub section (2) must be supported only if the conditions laid down in that proviso could be shown to have been complied with, namely, that the Government had formed the opinion that it was in the public interest to terminate such lease and three months ' notice had been given before such termination; and (iii) the third Proviso to sub s.(1) did not govern the second provisos. HELD: The third proviso deals with the termination Of rights created after July 1, 1945, one would have expected those conditions to be mentioned in the second schedule itself. [562 B] The scheme of section 20 is that the term of the leases should be renewed at the option of the lessee for one period not exceeding the duration of the original lease. The effect of this rule is that rights created before July 1. 1945, would be valid and enforceable by or against the Government without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the government to avoid the same. [563 C] In the present case the third provisos deal with the termina tion of rights created prior to July 1 1945, and the second sub section deals with termination of rights creating after July 31, 1945. The third Proviso deals with a termination of right created before the notified date. The first condition is that in the event of payment of compensation, on payment of compensa tion, and this repugnancy can be avoided, only by construing them as referring to different subjects. Then again there is in proviso (iii), an exception with reference to rights created over private lands; there is nothing corresponding to it in the third sub section.
